title: Add minimal TypeScript/Bun submission with no npm dependencies
body:
Adds a direct HTTP Bun 1.4.2/SQLite implementation with built-in routing, crypto and database support, 130 application/helper lines and no npm packages.

Reads query current data, every authenticated request verifies its JWT, and successful writes commit before responses. The fixed schema, WAL, synchronous=NORMAL and foreign keys are retained.

Completed responses retire connections at a budget of **60,000 open process descriptors**, reduced to leave 128 descriptors free under smaller inherited limits. Ordinary counts retain 75-second keep-alive; valid uploads finish and successful writes commit before retirement. Clients reconnect for their next request. Linux descriptor counts are sampled at most once per 100 ms after request work; EMFILE/ENFILE also triggers retirement. Platforms without /proc retain ordinary keep-alive without this Linux guard.

Validation of the final sources on Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64:

- All 42 official checks and the submission's additional API/concurrent duplicate-like checks passed.
- Fragmented/chunked uploads, 100 abandoned uploads, 100 resets after complete uploads, 1,800 pipelined responses under backpressure and 66-second original-socket reuse passed.
- 192 acknowledged creates and likes survived process-group SIGKILL/restart; 32 failed FK writes stayed isolated.
- At nofile=256, 64 retired responses, 32 committed writes/readbacks, completion of an interrupted Unicode upload and keep-alive recovery passed.
- A raw-socket burst exhausted descriptors before completing one request; its valid response drained fully and the server closed the socket.

The selected diagnostic served **70,000 logical users for a five-minute hold**, with **0 errors**, worst-shard p95/p99 **42.3/60.1 ms**, and sampled peak container memory **690.6 MiB**. The sum of process RSS high-water marks reached **156.8 MiB**; shared pages may be counted more than once.

This is one local ARM64 Docker trial on Apple M2 Pro, with one server CPU, 2 GiB RAM, no container swap, separate generator CPUs and a fresh seed. The C generator follows the request mix and think-time ranges in bench/load.js, with different PRNG/post text and no separate warm-up or ramp-down. Percentiles are the worst shard values. This establishes a selected passing load, not maximum capacity or an official x86_64 droplet score. Historical throughput/LOC comparisons remain measurements of their recorded baseline revisions.

[Architecture and reproduction](https://github.com/tbsvttr/twelve-dollar-server-challenge/blob/970d6079914330030add382d381e32bcb41ddb04/submissions/typescript-bun-tbsvttr/README.md) · [Source hashes and raw diagnostic/validation evidence](https://github.com/tbsvttr/twelve-dollar-server-challenge/blob/970d6079914330030add382d381e32bcb41ddb04/submissions/typescript-bun-tbsvttr/capacity-results.json)

Only submissions/typescript-bun-tbsvttr/ is changed. Generated binaries and dependency trees are excluded.

title: Add cpp-epoll-khalefa-ow submission (C++ / raw epoll, direct)
body:
Adds `submissions/cpp-epoll-khalefa-ow/`: a C++17 server on one hand-written epoll event loop, with SQLite compiled into the binary. No framework.

- **Nginx or direct:** direct, on `0.0.0.0:80`.
- **Stack:** GCC from Ubuntu 24.04 (`build-essential`), SQLite 3.53.4 amalgamation (downloaded by `build.sh`, sha256-pinned), OpenSSL `libcrypto` for SHA-256.
- **Tests:** `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 from a clean build.

## Design

- **One thread runs everything.** It handles all connections and runs every SQLite query inline. Each query is an index lookup that takes microseconds, so on one vCPU this beats handing work to other threads. A second thread only runs WAL checkpoints (`PASSIVE`, every 200 ms), so their fsync mostly stays off the event loop. SQLite's default auto-checkpoint stays on as a backstop to keep the WAL bounded.
- **Requests are parsed without copying.** They're read straight out of one shared 64 KiB read buffer, and a connection only gets its own buffer while a request is incomplete. An idle keep-alive connection is a small struct. Idle connections are closed after 120 s; the spec asks for at least 65.
- **The JWT is fully verified on every request**: HS256 only, constant-time comparison, `exp` and `nbf` checked. Only the HMAC key's inner and outer pads are computed once at startup.
- **Writes are durable before the response**: WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`, and every write is its own autocommit transaction. No group commit. Nothing is cached across requests: reads use only SQLite's page cache and `mmap`.

The README covers the full list of optimizations and the reasons for them.

## Local measurements (WSL2, server pinned to 1 core, k6 on the other cores)

These come from shortened runs (30 s ramp, 60 s hold), not the official 5-minute hold, so they're only a rough indication.

| VUs | p50 | p95 | p99 | Errors | Server CPU | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2,500 | 0.35 ms | 0.70 ms | 3.0 ms | 0% | 14% | 15 MB |
| 5,000 | 0.33 ms | 3.0 ms | 19.5 ms | 0% | 23% | 21 MB |
| 7,500 | 0.36 ms | 12.9 ms | 78 ms | 0% | 25% | 25 MB |

**Caveat at 7,500 VUs:** the first run at this level failed. The server stopped responding for about a minute while core 0 was 82% busy. I couldn't reproduce it: a rerun with monitoring passed cleanly at 25% CPU. My best guess is interference on the shared test machine, but I haven't confirmed that.

With the `bench/load.js` request mix, the server averages about 47 µs of CPU per request (user + kernel).

title: Add cpp-epoll_inmem-khalefa-ow submission (C++ / raw epoll v2, direct)
body:
Adds `submissions/cpp-epoll_inmem-khalefa-ow/`: a second version of `cpp-epoll-khalefa-ow` (#8). It's the same hand-written C++17 epoll server with SQLite compiled in, tuned for tail latency and per-request kernel time. No framework.

- **Nginx or direct:** direct, on `0.0.0.0:80`.
- **Stack:** GCC from Ubuntu 24.04 (`build-essential`), SQLite 3.53.4 amalgamation (downloaded by `build.sh`, sha256-pinned), OpenSSL `libcrypto` for SHA-256.
- **Tests:** `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 from a clean build.

## Changes from v1

- **Fully single-threaded, `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`.** File locks are taken once and the WAL index lives in heap memory instead of a shared `-shm` mapping. This replaces v1's background checkpoint thread. SQLite is built with `SQLITE_THREADSAFE=0`.
- **Checkpoints run between event-loop batches, not inside a commit.** A WAL hook records the WAL size, and the loop checkpoints at 1,000 frames after the current batch of responses has been sent, so no write's response waits on checkpoint fsyncs.
- **500-page cache instead of 32 MiB.** Reads go through `mmap`. SQLite scans the cache's hash table on every commit, which at 32 MiB was ~13% of user CPU.
- **SIMD JSON escaping** (16 bytes at a time): ~41 ns instead of ~300 ns for a 300-byte body.
- **Prewarm at startup.** Every table and index is read once through `mmap`, so early requests don't stall on page faults. These pages are the OS page cache (rule 5), not an app cache. RSS reads ~220 MB because it includes the mapped file; anonymous memory stays around 1 MB.
- **Bounded accepts** (64 per loop iteration), so a ramp-up burst can't hold up in-flight requests.

Unchanged from v1: JWT fully verified on every request, writes durable before the response (WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`, one autocommit transaction per write), nothing cached across requests. The README has the details.

title: Add Erlang + Cowboy + SQLite submission
body:
Adds a standalone Erlang/Cowboy/SQLite implementation of the five challenge endpoints. OTP JSON and crypto handle serialization and HS256 JWT verification; a database owner process serializes prepared SQLite statements. Pinned Cowboy/Cowlib/Ranch/esqlite sources and SQLite are SHA256-verified, and the build uses erlc and the C compiler.

Reads query current SQLite data, authenticated requests verify their JWT, and successful writes commit before responses. WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`, foreign keys and the fixed schema are retained.

At high connection counts, idle keep-alive sockets consume descriptors and memory. The server retires connections after completed responses at a budget of **32,000 open connections**. Clients reconnect for the next request; uploads and pending commits finish before retirement. Smaller inherited descriptor limits reduce the budget with a reserve of 128. Ordinary connection counts retain the 75-second keep-alive timeout.

Ranch accepts up to 60,000 connections with a 4,096 listen backlog, adjusted for inherited file/port limits. A 100 ms sampler publishes its connection count. The `+hmbs 1024` runtime flag collects discarded response binaries sooner on mostly idle connection processes; it changes the GC trigger rather than imposing a hard memory limit.

Validation of the updated sources:

- 42/42 official API checks, 62 additional HTTP checks and 16 concurrent duplicate likes passed on Linux ARM64.
- Fragmented/chunked uploads, abandoned requests, 1,800 pipelined responses under backpressure and reuse of the original socket after 66 idle seconds passed.
- 192 acknowledged creates and likes survived SIGKILL/restart; 32 failed foreign-key writes stayed isolated.
- With server `nofile=256`, the pressure regression verified 64 retired connections, 32 committed writes/readbacks, completion of an unfinished Unicode upload and recovery of keep-alive after pressure subsided.

The selected local diagnostic served **30,000 logical users for a 5-minute hold**, with **zero errors**, worst-shard p95/p99 **8.6/21.0 ms**, peak process RSS **1284.6 MiB**, and sampled peak container memory **1718.5 MiB**.

These are single-trial diagnostics on Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 under Docker Desktop on Apple M2 Pro, with one server CPU, 2 GiB RAM, no container swap, separate load-generator CPUs and a fresh seed copy. The C epoll generator follows the k6 request mix and think-time ranges, with different random generation/post text and no separate warm-up or ramp-down. Reported percentiles are the worst shard values. This establishes a selected passing local load, not maximum capacity or the official x86_64 droplet score. Previous throughput comparisons remain labeled as measurements of their recorded baseline revisions.

[Architecture and reproduction](<https://github.com/tbsvttr/twelve-dollar-server-challenge/blob/83a51a2dd6b82434d01da25c9471725946e741a9/submissions/erlang-cowboy-tbsvttr/README.md>) · [Capacity evidence, source hashes and validation logs](<https://github.com/tbsvttr/twelve-dollar-server-challenge/blob/83a51a2dd6b82434d01da25c9471725946e741a9/submissions/erlang-cowboy-tbsvttr/capacity-results.json>) · [Descriptor-pressure regression](<https://github.com/tbsvttr/twelve-dollar-server-challenge/blob/83a51a2dd6b82434d01da25c9471725946e741a9/submissions/erlang-cowboy-tbsvttr/tests/pressure_regression.py>)

title: Add cpp-epoll-memstore-khalefa-ow submission (C++ / epoll, custom in-memory store — NOT SQLite-based)
body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **This is not a SQLite-based solution.** The server stores its data in a custom in-memory store with its own WAL and snapshot files. It never opens `$SQLITE_PATH` while serving and doesn't link SQLite. SQLite is used only once, before the server starts: a separate `bin/import` program converts the seed `feed.db` into the store's own format.
>
> That breaks **rule 2** (the database is SQLite) and **rule 5** (no in-memory copies of tables), and the README says so up front. I'm submitting it as a reference point for how much of the per-request cost of my SQLite entry (#9) is SQLite. Please judge it as such, or close it if it shouldn't be listed.

Adds `submissions/cpp-epoll-memstore-khalefa-ow/`. It's the same hand-written C++17 epoll server as #9 (same HTTP parser, JWT check and JSON code). Only the data layer is different.

- **Nginx or direct:** direct.
- **Stack:** GCC from Ubuntu 24.04 (`build-essential`), OpenSSL `libcrypto` for SHA-256. The SQLite 3.53.4 amalgamation (sha256-pinned) is compiled into `bin/import` only.
- **Tests:** `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 from a clean build.

## The store (`src/store.hpp`)

- **Posts:** an array indexed by id. Each entry holds the post's JSON already rendered up to `"like_count":`, plus a like counter. `GET /posts/:id` is an array lookup and a `memcpy`.
- **Feed:** post ids kept sorted by `(created_at, id)`. `GET /feed` reads the last 20.
- **Likes:** an open-addressing hash set of `(user, post)` keys that answers "already liked?". The count lives on the post.

## Durability

- Every write is appended to an app-specific WAL of CRC-checked records, with one `write()` per event-loop batch. No response from a batch is sent before its records are written.
- **The default matches SQLite's WAL mode with `synchronous=NORMAL`.** The WAL is `fdatasync`'d before a snapshot takes it over, the same way SQLite syncs before a checkpoint.
- **`WAL_SYNC=full` matches `synchronous=FULL`,** using group commit on a sync thread. A write's response waits for its `fdatasync`, but reads don't.
- **Compaction:** a `fork()`ed child writes snapshots from a copy-on-write image while the server keeps serving.
- **Recovery:** the server maps the snapshot, replays the WAL, and drops a torn tail. Startup takes about 0.2–0.5 s; the first start's import takes about 2 s.
- **Tested:** `kill -9` with writes in the WAL, during a snapshot, and after one finished, plus a torn WAL record. In every case the feed and like counts after restart were identical.

## Local measurements (WSL2 laptop, server pinned to 1 core, client on the other cores)

Server CPU per request, compared with my SQLite entry #9 (user / total µs):

| endpoint | SQLite (#9) | this store |
|---|---|---|
| feed | 47.0 / 65.6 | 2.8 / 18.8 |
| like | 35.0 / 80.1 | 4.5 / 18.5 |
| `load.js` mix | 21.0 / 36.6 | 2.4 / 12.3 |

- **`bench/load.js` (30 s ramp, 60 s hold):** both servers pass every level this machine can generate, up to 12,500 VUs, at 5–10% CPU. At those rates the two can't be told apart; tail latency on this machine is dominated by environment stalls.
- **Closed-loop saturation with the same mix:** about 17–18k req/s at 39% CPU, against about 14k req/s at 76% for #9. The client was the limit, not the server.

These are short local runs, not the official 5-minute hold.

title: [Rust] Tokio + Axum + Rusqlite
body:
The $12 server challenge API in Rust.

|                |                                                                                       |
|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Language       | Rust 1.99 (edition 2024)                                                              |
| HTTP           | axum 0.8.9 (tokio + hyper, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive)                                       |
| SQLite         | rusqlite 0.40.2 (`bundled`, compiled into the binary)                                 |
| JWT            | jsonwebtoken 11.1.0 (`rust_crypto`, pure Rust)                                        |
| JSON           | serde_json, response structs field-ordered to match the spec                          |
| Allocator      | tikv-jemallocator                                                                     |
| **Deployment** | **Behind Nginx** — serves `127.0.0.1:3000`, Nginx (`bench/nginx.conf`) fronts port 80 |


This solution implements an approach I've used in other applications. Single writer thread - writes are queued via bounded channel and batched optimistically to reduce the `fsync` cost.  

All handlers use structs that derive serialize/deserialize so the responses imitate what a real application would do, instead of hard-coding precomputed responses.

The solution uses the jsonwebtoken crate, something a real app would use, instead of doing manual token handling to game the benchmark.

Load tests results on my linux box:

- `memory_limit=-1`: in BASE mode Swoole allocates each connection's 64 KiB receive buffer from PHP's allocator, so a finite limit kills the worker at about 8,000 open connections even though real RSS is far lower.

Tested in a clean Ubuntu 24.04 container replicating CI (`install.sh` as root, `test/run.sh` as a normal user) on x86_64 and arm64: 42/42 passed. Local `bench/load.js` results (1 CPU, 2 GB container, 5-minute hold) are in the submission README: 20,000 users with 0 errors, p99 4.4 ms, 839 MB RSS.

title: Add Zig/uSockets submission with SQLite group commit
body:
Adds a direct HTTP/1.1 implementation in Zig 0.17.0 with uSockets, picohttpparser and SQLite 3.53.4. Writes share an event-loop transaction; responses, including reads that observed those writes, wait for COMMIT. Failed commits roll back and return HTTP 500. Dependencies are pinned and SHA256-verified.

Reads query current SQLite data, authenticated requests verify their JWT, and successful writes commit before responses. WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`, foreign keys and the fixed schema are retained.

At high connection counts, idle keep-alive sockets consume descriptors and memory. The server retires connections after completed responses at a budget of **60,000 open connections**. Clients reconnect for the next request; uploads and pending commits finish before retirement. Smaller inherited descriptor limits reduce the budget with a reserve of 128. Ordinary connection counts retain the 75-second keep-alive timeout.

The uSockets open/close callbacks maintain the count, and completed response bytes drain before socket closure. Interim `100 Continue` responses keep the upload connection open.

Validation of the updated sources:

- 42/42 official API checks, 62 additional HTTP checks and 16 concurrent duplicate likes passed on Linux ARM64.
- Fragmented/chunked uploads, abandoned requests, 1,800 pipelined responses under backpressure and reuse of the original socket after 66 idle seconds passed.
- 192 acknowledged creates and likes survived SIGKILL/restart; 32 failed foreign-key writes stayed isolated.
- With server `nofile=256`, the pressure regression verified 64 retired connections, 32 committed writes/readbacks, completion of an unfinished Unicode upload and recovery of keep-alive after pressure subsided.

The selected local diagnostic served **70,000 logical users for a 1-minute hold**, with **zero errors**, worst-shard p95/p99 **4.1/18.6 ms**, peak process RSS **65.6 MiB**, and sampled peak container memory **599.9 MiB**.

These are single-trial diagnostics on Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 under Docker Desktop on Apple M2 Pro, with one server CPU, 2 GiB RAM, no container swap, separate load-generator CPUs and a fresh seed copy. The C epoll generator follows the k6 request mix and think-time ranges, with different random generation/post text and no separate warm-up or ramp-down. Reported percentiles are the worst shard values. This establishes a selected passing local load, not maximum capacity or the official x86_64 droplet score. Previous throughput comparisons remain labeled as measurements of their recorded baseline revisions.

title: Add c-iouring-raoz submission (C, io_uring, direct)
body:
This pull request adds one folder: `submissions/c-iouring-raoz`.

**Language and framework:** C, with no framework. The HTTP/1.1 server uses io_uring directly, and SQLite is compiled into the binary.

**Nginx or direct:** Direct. The server listens on `0.0.0.0:80`.

## How it works

- One event loop accepts connections, reads requests and sends responses in batches.
- SQLite runs on the same thread. The writes of one batch share one commit, and no response goes out before that commit.
- Each socket goes into an io_uring file table. Thus the server can hold more than 65,535 connections with `LimitNOFILE=65535`.
- If free memory gets low, the server stops accepting new connections and keeps the connections that it has.

## Results

I tested on a DigitalOcean `s-1vcpu-2gb` droplet with Ubuntu 24.04. The server ran as a systemd service, and the box was not tuned.

| Users | Requests/s | Errors | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100,000 | 10,600 | 0 | 15 ms | 28 ms |
| 125,000 | 13,200 | 0 | 166 ms | 5.7 s |

The limit on this droplet is about 110,000 users. The CPU sets the limit. With k6 and `bench/load.js` on AWS, 60,000 users gave 0 errors and a p99 of 31 ms.

k6 needs about 280 KB of memory for each user. For the larger runs, I used a small load generator that follows the same user loop as `bench/load.js`. The source is in `tests/loadgen.c`.

## Tests

`test/test.sh` passes 42 of 42 checks. The folder also has more tests in C, for HTTP framing, JWT claims, commit failure and crash recovery. `build.sh` does not build them. To run them, use `make -C tests check` after `build.sh`.

title: Add cpp-drogon-hendy643 submission
body:
Adds `submissions/cpp-drogon-hendy643/`.

- **Stack:** C++26 (clang 20, Ubuntu 24.04's `clang-20`), Drogon 1.9.13, Glaze 8.0.0, SQLite 3.45.1 through its C API (Ubuntu's `libsqlite3`), OpenSSL for the HMAC. Drogon and Glaze are pinned by git tag in `CMakeLists.txt`; everything else is an Ubuntu package. Built with `-O3 -march=native -flto`, linked with lld, release binary stripped.
- **Direct** (no Nginx): serves `0.0.0.0:80` itself. It also runs behind `bench/nginx.conf` on `127.0.0.1:3000` (see the compose profiles below).

## How it works

- One event-loop thread per CPU in the affinity mask, so one thread on the droplet. Each thread has its own SQLite connection and prepared statements, and queries run inline on the loop.
- WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`, autocommit, so every 201 is committed before the response is sent. Every request reads from SQLite; nothing is cached across requests.
- HS256 verified by hand on every request: one OpenSSL HMAC and a constant-time compare.
- Routing is a single `registerSyncAdvice` that bypasses Drogon's router. Responses are written with Glaze into a reused buffer.
- A like is one `INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`; the post-existence lookup only runs when nothing was inserted.
- Drogon (Trantor) aborts when `accept()` fails with `EMFILE`, so the process raises its soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` to the hard limit and refuses new connections before it would run out. It is an in-process setting only (rule 11).

## Tests

- `install.sh` as root and `build.sh` as a normal user in a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container; `test/test.sh` passes 42/42 against it, direct and behind `bench/nginx.conf`. Also 42/42 through `test/run.sh` on my machine.
- Glaze is held at 8.0.0 because 8.1 and later need CMake 3.31 and Ubuntu 24.04 ships 3.28.

## Local numbers

Not a droplet run, so please don't read these as the score.

- **Hardware:** Ryzen 9 5900X (a faster core than a droplet vCPU), 32 GB RAM
- **Limits:** Docker confines the server to one CPU thread and 2 GB RAM, no swap
- **Load:** `bench/load.js`, 2,500 users, 30 s ramp then a 90 s hold, k6 on the same machine pinned to other cores
- **Correctness:** `test/test.sh` passes 42/42 in both modes

| | Direct | Behind `bench/nginx.conf` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Requests | 33,861 | 33,886 |
| Failed | 0 | 0 |
| avg | 106 µs | 204 µs |
| median | 100 µs | 187 µs |
| p95 | 159 µs | 302 µs |
| p99 | 220 µs | 420 µs |
| max | 7.6 ms | 9.1 ms |

## Extra

The folder also contains a `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` (`direct` and `nginx` profiles) and `docker/nginx.conf`, for reproducing the droplet's limits locally. They are not used by `install.sh`, `build.sh` or `start.sh`. The compose file reads `../../bench/nginx.conf` read-only and changes nothing outside the folder.

title: Add cpp-eastl-io_uring-pgo-hendy643 submission (C++, EASTL, io_uring, PGO SQLite)
body:
Adds submissions/cpp-eastl-io_uring-pgo-hendy643/.

- Stack: C++23, Ubuntu 24.04's default GCC (13.3), -O3 -march=native -flto=auto, stripped. No framework: a hand-written single-threaded io_uring server on liburing. EASTL 3.27.01 where it covers what's needed. JSON scanner and writer are hand-written. SQLite 3.53.4 is built from the amalgamation (SHA-256 checked) with PGO. OpenSSL, liburing and GoogleTest come from apt; EASTL is pinned by git tag.
- Direct (no Nginx): serves 0.0.0.0:80 itself.
- Needs io_uring: kernel 6.0+, kernel.io_uring_disabled=0, no seccomp profile blocking it. If it can't set the ring up it exits with the reason. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks it, so a CI container needs --security-opt seccomp=unconfined.

How it works

- One thread. Multishot recv into a shared provided-buffer ring, 256 accepts kept armed, one SQLite connection with prepared statements, queries inline on the loop.
- The loop waits for 128 completions or 6 ms once load is non-trivial (4+ completions in the last pass). That cuts syscalls and makes group commits larger. It adds latency (p99 about 7 ms at 40k users) but costs about 8 µs less CPU per request than waking per completion.
- Connections live in io_uring registered file tables, so they don't count against LimitNOFILE. A table can't exceed RLIMIT_NOFILE, so there are 5 rings of 65,535 slots driven by the one thread: 327,675 connections. Past that, the server evicts a connection that was just served and is idle. With the benchmark's think-time loop LRU would evict the one needed next. Kernels without direct file tables fall back to normal fds with LRU eviction.
- Writes in a batch share one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction. Every response produced while it's open, reads included, waits for the commit, so nothing uncommitted is visible (rule 6). synchronous=NORMAL, WAL, locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE.
- HS256 verified on every request with the HMAC key pads hashed once at startup. Nothing is cached (rule 5).
- The feed is three range scans (newest ids, likes for that id range, rows for that id range) and falls back to the reference query if the ids aren't consecutive. Every response still comes from queries run for that request.
- No heap allocation on the request path; a unit test counts allocations and expects zero.

Tests

- 72 unit tests in build.sh, including differential fuzzing of the JSON scanner against yyjson and of the HTTP parser against a scalar reference, and a differential test of the feed against the reference query.
- test/test.sh passes 42/42 locally, under ASan/UBSan (no findings), and in a clean ubuntu:24.04 container built with install.sh as root and build.sh as a normal user.

Not a droplet run, so please don't read these as the score.

- Hardware: Ryzen 9 5900X (a faster core than a droplet vCPU), 32 GB RAM
- Limits: Docker confines the server to one CPU thread and 2 GB RAM, no swap, nofile 65535, host network
- Load: k6 with bench/load.js up to 65k users (90 s hold). Above that, the raw-socket generator from #26 (tests/loadgen.c, not part of this PR). Holds are shorter than the scored 5 minutes.

| Generator   |   Users | CPU per request |     p95 |     p99 | Failed |
|-------------|--------:|----------------:|--------:|--------:|-------:|
| k6          |  40,000 |         17.2 µs |  6.6 ms |  7.0 ms |  0.00% |
| k6          |  65,000 |         16.8 µs |  7.3 ms |  7.9 ms |  0.00% |
| raw sockets | 100,000 |         11.2 µs |  7.5 ms |  7.8 ms |  0.00% |
| raw sockets | 200,000 |         10.3 µs |  8.8 ms |  9.5 ms |  0.00% |
| raw sockets | 250,000 |         10.4 µs | 10.1 ms | 11.1 ms |  0.00% |

The two generators' CPU figures aren't comparable: the raw-socket one moves some loopback cost onto its own cores.

Not tested:
- Above about 262k users: this machine's nf_conntrack_max is 262,144 and the kernel drops new connections past that, so I can't measure higher here.
- Eviction at 327k: eviction was only exercised at small scale (10,000 descriptors, 70,000 users, 0.03% failures).
- Limit search: I have not run the doubling search or a 5-minute hold.

Extra

The folder also has a Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml and pgo/ (the SQLite PGO build and its training driver). Only pgo/ is used by build.sh; the Docker files exist for reproducing the droplet's limits locally. Nothing outside the folder is changed.

body:
Adds `submissions/java-spring-boot-nb-99/`: Java 25 on Spring Boot 4 with Spring WebFlux, serving clients directly on Netty, with SQLite through sqlite-jdbc.

| | |
|---|---|
| Language | Java 25: Eclipse Temurin 25.0.1+8, official tarball, SHA-256 checked by `install.sh` |
| Framework | Spring Boot 4.0.3, Spring WebFlux 7.0.5 on Reactor Netty 1.3.3 |
| SQLite | Xerial sqlite-jdbc 3.53.4.0, which bundles SQLite 3.53.4 |
| Build | Maven 3.9.11, SHA-512 checked; the POM pins every dependency |
| Nginx or direct | Direct on `0.0.0.0:80` |

**What makes it fast** (the submission README explains each change):
- **No Nginx.** Clients talk to Netty directly, which saves the proxy's CPU and a second HTTP parse. An idle keep-alive connection holds no buffers.
- **SQLite writes the JSON.** `json_object` and `json_group_array` return the complete feed and post bodies, and the app sends those bytes as they are. Jackson only writes likes, new posts, health, and errors.
- **Statements prepared once per connection.** They cache plans, never results.
- **One writer, three readers.** Every write goes through one connection, so writes wait in a Java queue instead of sleeping in SQLite's busy handler. Reads use three `query_only` connections. Each connection has its own thread, away from Netty's event loops.
- **No extra query per insert.** sqlite-jdbc's generated-key lookup is off; new ids come from `RETURNING`.
- **JVM.** Serial GC and a 1.25 GiB heap cap.

**Rules:** every request reads SQLite, with no response or result caches. WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`, and each 201 is sent after its own commit (no group commit). Every authenticated request verifies the HS256 signature and `exp`.

**Testing:**
- `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 in a clean Ubuntu 24.04 container: `install.sh` as root, then build, start, and tests as a normal user.
- `build.sh` runs 27 HTTP integration tests, including exact response bytes, escaping and Unicode in the SQLite-built JSON, concurrent duplicate likes, and commits visible from another connection.

**Local load tests.** These ran on Kubernetes with the app pod limited to 1 vCPU and 2 GiB and k6 running `bench/load.js` from another node, so they compare the two versions rather than predict the droplet's score. Each row is the latest run of that version:

| Version | Result |
|---|---|
| Spring MVC with the same optimizations | 31,750 users held for 5 minutes: p95 395 ms, p99 729 ms, no errors |
| WebFlux (this PR) | 38,000 users passed a 1-minute probe: p95 21 ms, p99 46 ms. The 5-minute hold at 38,000 failed (p99 2,972 ms), and the one at 37,750 stopped on a k6 error |

title: Go: fib/rr/ggen/sqlite
body:
## Summary

Adds a Go 1.27 server built with:
- [fib](https://github.com/lesismal/fib) - superfast stdlib-compatible networking library;
- [rr](https://github.com/sirkostya009/rr) - codegen HTTP router;
- [ggen](https://github.com/sirkostya009/ggen) - codegen JSON with decode-time validation, AVX2 codecs;
- [crawshaw.io/sqlite](https://github.com/crawshaw/sqlite) - cgo, bundled SQLite compiled from source.

It serves directly on `HOST:PORT`, without Nginx, and passes `test/test.sh` 42/42 on a fresh seed copy.

## Architecture

I tried keeping the architecture and code organization close to how I would normally create a stable and clean project for long-term development: typical 3-layer architecture with of an api, a service and a repository. The only cheat in my opinion is the repository layer: too much manual query building going on (I think most of the churn can be delegated to codegen tools, but I haven't figured out the right abstractions for that yet). `rr` and `ggen` are my own inventions, so this stack is only used by me... It does its work pretty fast tho.

## How it works

Three layer architecture, API parsing and validating wire shapes, verifying JWT tokens, delegating to the service layer which only calls into repository. The latter itself operates on a shared, read-write db instance with locking handled by the repository layer.

## Optimizations

The Go runtime is pinned for 1 vCPU and 2 GB with `GOMAXPROCS=1` and GC % set to 400 with up to a 768 MB `GOMEMLIMIT`. The folder's README covers versions, optimizations and known untested edge cases.

SQLite runs in `locking_mode= exclusive` and `synchronous=NORMAL`.

title: Add go-gnet-Haris0059 submission
body:
## What
Adds a Go submission (`submissions/go-gnet-Haris0059/`). It serves port 80 directly (no Nginx) from a single gnet event
loop and uses a small cgo shim over a pinned SQLite 3.53.4. SQLite builds the JSON responses.

## Why
On 1 vCPU with tens of thousands of keep-alive users, the limits are memory per connection and CPU per request:
- **Event loop instead of a goroutine per connection.** gnet watches every socket from one epoll loop, so idle
  connections cost almost nothing (~100–130 MB RSS at 40–60k connections, vs ~930 MB with fasthttp at 40k).
- **One cgo call per query instead of `database/sql`.** A small C shim binds, steps, copies the result out and resets in
  one call, on one connection with statements prepared once.
- **JSON built inside SQLite** (`json_object` + `group_concat`), so `/feed` and `/posts/:id` are one row each.

Rules: statements are reused, but no data is cached (rule 5). WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`, and each write commits before
its response (rule 6). The SQLite source is downloaded by `build.sh` at a pinned version with a sha256 check, and gnet is
pinned in `go.mod` (rule 10).

## Changes
- `main.go`: routing, handlers, hand-rolled HS256 JWT check on every request, input validation, GC settings.

body:
Adds `submissions/c-h2o-einhornimmond/`.

  - **Stack:** C (GNU C11) built with zig 0.15.2 (`zig cc`, `ReleaseFast`). [h2o](https://github.com/h2o/h2o) as a
  library (evloop, epoll), SQLite 3.53.2, libsodium for HS256, [arnm](https://github.com/gradido/arnm) for arenas
  and JSON. LibreSSL and zlib are linked by h2o. All dependencies are pinned with hashes in `build.zig.zon` and
  built from source.
  - **Direct** (no Nginx): serves `0.0.0.0:80` itself. The same binary also runs behind `bench/nginx.conf` on
  `127.0.0.1:3000`.

  The server is written for this challenge, but on a stack that is being built for another project (the C fast path
  of [gradido-unicorn](https://github.com/gradido/gradido-unicorn), still in development). It was not chosen for this benchmark, so this entry shows how far that
  stack goes on the box.

  ## How it works

  - One h2o event loop per core, so one loop on the droplet. Reads run on the loop thread on its own read-only
  SQLite connection with prepared statements.
  - Writes go through a queue to one writer thread that owns the write connection. It commits everything that queued
  up in one transaction (group commit); no response is sent before its commit.
  - `/feed` is three range scans in one read transaction instead of the correlated subqueries, with the reference
  query as fallback.
  - Every token's signature is verified on every request. Nothing is cached across requests. WAL with
  `synchronous=NORMAL`, schema unchanged.

  ## Results

  Measured on my development machine (Ryzen 7 5700G), server pinned to one core, load over
  loopback with the load generator from #26 (`tests/loadgen.c`):

  | Users | Requests/s | Errors | p95 | p99 | CPU | RSS |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 60,000 | 6,350 | 0 | 0.5 ms | 2.0 ms | 36% of the core | 129 MB |

  Behind Nginx, 15,000 users ran with 0 errors at 20% of the core for Nginx and the server together. More numbers
  and the design notes are in the submission README.

  ## Tests

  `test/run.sh` passes 42/42. I also ran the CI steps in a clean Ubuntu 24.04 container (Docker) limited to 1 CPU and 2 GB
  (`install.sh` as root, `build.sh` and `test/run.sh` as a normal user): the build takes about 4 minutes, the tests
  pass 42/42, and the server is healthy in under a second.

title: Add python-fastapi-granian-shawal-mbalire submission
body:
Adds `submissions/python-fastapi-granian-shawal-mbalire/`: FastAPI served by Granian (Rust HTTP server), **direct** on `0.0.0.0:80`, on Python 3.11.17 from python-build-standalone (pinned by release and SHA-256).

## Highlights

- **SQLite renders every response.** `json_object` / `group_concat` build the documents, so Python only joins byte strings (PR #13's idea).
- **FastAPI without its per-request machinery** (PR #10): no dependency solving, no `Request`/`Response` objects, no middleware stack, and no Starlette routing. HTTP requests go straight from the app to a small dispatcher (an exact path lookup plus a `/posts/` split); only the lifespan goes through FastAPI's router. FastAPI 0.143's native telemetry is off, because it cost three `os.environ` lookups per request.
- **Granian's Rust task implementation** (`--task-impl rust`, which Granian calls experimental and runs only on Python 3.11): 3–7% less CPU per request than Python 3.15 with asyncio tasks, in alternating runs.
- **Group commit.** Writes in one event-loop pass share a single `COMMIT`, and every response waits for its commit (PRs #25, #22, #15). One `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` WAL connection, `synchronous=NORMAL`, and a passive checkpoint once a second, off the commit path.
- **`--backpressure 65535`.** Granian's default (4096) caps *open connections*. In direct mode every user holds one, so with the default, 20k users got 22% timeouts while the CPU sat 7% busy.
- **Descriptor guard** (idea from PR #13, budget from PR #71). Every 50 ms the server reads the kernel's count of open TCP sockets; while 61,439 or more are open (the 65,535 limit minus 4,096), responses carry `Connection: close`. This keeps the server under the descriptor limit without dropping connections from a full accept queue.
- JWT HS256 is verified by hand on every request; no caching across requests.

## Verification

- `test/run.sh`: **42/42 pass**, also in a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container with `install.sh` and `build.sh`. 50 unit tests (stdlib `unittest`) pass.

## Results (not a droplet score)

`just bench linux`, on an Apple M-series machine whose cores are faster than a droplet vCPU. Terraform (`infra/iac/bench/`) creates the server (1 CPU, 1792 MiB, no swap, nofile 65535, built with this entry's `install.sh` / `build.sh`) and four load-generator containers running PR #14's C generator (the `load.js` user loop). They talk over a Docker bridge, not loopback, and the server's CPU pays for its own network work. The bench keeps the VM's CPU clock steady, which earlier runs did not (see the README).

**120,000 users hold for the full 5 minutes** with the submitted build: p95 15 ms, p99 107 ms, 0 errors, no dropped connections, 65% of CPU 0, 56 µs of server CPU per request, peak memory 1,560 MiB. 130k is the edge (it passed 5 minutes in one of three tries on the earlier 3.15 build); 140k fails. Past ~65k users the descriptor limit forces reconnects, and accepting them is what runs out.

Six entries alternated run by run at 40,000 users (3 rounds, 0 errors for all; measured on the earlier 3.15 build, which is 3–7% more expensive than the submitted one):

| Entry | Server CPU per request | CPU 0 busy | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| #71 Ruby async | 36.9–39.0 µs (37.9) | 17–18% | 3.5–4.2 ms |
| #84 PyPy + raw epoll | 39.2–42.6 µs (41.1) | 20–21% | 3.2–8.4 ms |
| **this entry** | **59.5–66.2 µs (62.4)** | **24–26%** | **6.4–10.8 ms** |
| #10 lean FastAPI (droplet 22k) | 66.4–77.1 µs (71.2) | 25–30% | 4.1–13.5 ms |
| #13 Granian RSGI | 90.7–102.8 µs (97.9) | 36–40% | 19.9–24.4 ms |
| #1 FastAPI + uvicorn (droplet 11k) | 107.6–114.1 µs (110.6) | 41–43% | 6.9–11.4 ms |

**Expected droplet score: around or above 22,000 users, not measured.** This entry uses about 12% less CPU per request than #10, which scored 22k on the droplet. An earlier version of this description claimed 80k from a loopback benchmark; that number was wrong, and so were the per-request numbers measured before the bench's clock was controlled. The README has the details and method.

One question for the maintainer: `build.sh` downloads a prebuilt CPython from python-build-standalone (pinned by SHA-256) instead of using Ubuntu's. Is that acceptable under the rules?

Only `submissions/python-fastapi-granian-shawal-mbalire/` is added.

body:
Swift 6.2.1 + Hummingbird 2.26.0 + system libsqlite3 via direct C interop + swift-crypto for HS256 JWTs. Serves `0.0.0.0:80` directly (no Nginx) — skips the 14–20% CPU Nginx + gzip cost from the video.

- WAL readers on a small lock-guarded connection pool run inline on the event-loop threads (readers never block the writer)

- Prepared statements created once per connection; error responses are prebuilt constants

title: Add go-stdlib-vkrishna03 submission (Go standard library, epoll, SQLite; direct on :80)
body:
Adds `submissions/go-stdlib-vkrishna03/`: **Go 1.27.2, standard library only, serving directly on `0.0.0.0:80`** (no Nginx).

- **One level-triggered epoll event loop** with a small HTTP/1.1 parser (keep-alive, pipelining, split packets, `100-continue`, backpressure). An idle connection costs ~100 bytes in user space. Running out of descriptors at `LimitNOFILE` pauses accept instead of spinning.
- **SQLite 3.53.4 compiled in** from the official amalgamation (`build.sh` checks its sha256) with the recommended compile-time options (`THREADSAFE=0`, `DEFAULT_MEMSTATUS=0`, `OMIT_*`). It's called through a thin cgo layer: persistent statements, one cgo call per row, zero allocations per request.
- **Feed as three range scans:** ids from the `created_at` index, then posts with their authors in `[lo, hi]`, then like counts in `[lo, hi]`. This replaces the reference query's 60 lookups whenever the 20 newest ids are adjacent, which is almost always; otherwise the reference query runs. The output is byte-identical.
- `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` (−17% CPU), WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`, checkpoints every 10k pages, no mmap.
- Rules: every request reads SQLite and every JWT is verified (HS256, `exp`/`nbf`). `INSERT ... RETURNING` runs to `SQLITE_DONE` (commit) before a 201 is sent.

**Tests:** `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 on Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64 and arm64), plus 58 extra raw-socket HTTP/JSON/JWT edge cases. `PRAGMA integrity_check` is `ok` after 60k-user runs.

**Local load** (Docker on an M3, server pinned to one core with 2 GB and `nofile=65535`, `bench/load.js`'s user loop). I calibrated against real droplet runs (the official #1 result and #38's report): a droplet vCPU is about 0.6 of this core.

| Load | Errors | p95 | p99 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 60k users, full core (~47% CPU) | 0 | 2.3–2.7 ms | 18–30 ms |
| 64k users, throttled to 0.5 core (harsher than a droplet) | 0 | 0.16–0.6 s | 0.25–0.92 s |
| No think time, realistic mix (wrk) | — | 125,900 req/s at 7.5 µs CPU each | |

The README also lists what was measured and rejected: io_uring in pure Go (same CPU as epoll), batched wake-ups, `SO_REUSEPORT` processes (+12% CPU), small socket buffers, and SQL-built JSON.

- **Durable writes:** `journal_mode=WAL` with `synchronous=NORMAL` (Rule 6). Inserts step to `SQLITE_DONE` before responding 201.

This is a selected passing local load, not an official DigitalOcean score or demonstrated maximum. Run settings, runtime/image/source/workload identifiers, earlier trials and measurement boundaries are recorded in `PERFORMANCE.md` and `performance-results.json`.

Add a Go server on one epoll loop that serves 0.0.0.0:80 directly, without Nginx. It calls SQLite 3.53.4 through a small cgo binding and has no dependencies beyond the Go standard library.

Writes use group commit. Each epoll batch shares one transaction, and the batch's responses are held until COMMIT succeeds. SQLite runs in exclusive locking mode with WAL and synchronous=NORMAL. test/run.sh passes all 42 checks on x86_64 and arm64. The scripts in tests/ check durability under SIGKILL, failed commits, WAL growth and behaviour at the descriptor limit.

title: Add kotlin-ktor-graalvm-noamm9 submission
body:
Adds `submissions/kotlin-ktor-graalvm-noamm9`: Kotlin + Ktor (CIO) compiled to a **GraalVM native image**, on SQLite through sqlite-jdbc.

## Nginx or direct

**Direct is preferred**: run it on `0.0.0.0:80` without Nginx. The native binary has a small, flat memory footprint (about 250 MiB peak RSS at 10,000 users in my local load test), so it can hold the keep-alive connections itself, and the single vCPU isn't shared with Nginx.

It works behind the challenge's Nginx too: just start it with `HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=3000`. Nothing else changes.

## How to run

```bash
sudo bash install.sh   # GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1 tarball into /opt/graalvm (SHA-256 checked) + build-essential, zlib1g-dev
bash build.sh          # Gradle compiles, exits, then native-image builds build/native/nativeCompile/velox

# direct (preferred)
SQLITE_PATH=/path/to/feed.db JWT_SECRET=twelve-dollar-challenge HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=80 bash start.sh

# behind Nginx
SQLITE_PATH=/path/to/feed.db JWT_SECRET=twelve-dollar-challenge HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=3000 bash start.sh
```

`start.sh` execs the binary in the foreground and is configured only by `SQLITE_PATH`, `JWT_SECRET`, `HOST` and `PORT`. Startup takes about 50 ms.

**Build time on the droplet:** expect about 8 minutes on 1 vCPU. The build is set up to fit the 2 GB box with no swap:
- Gradle compiles Kotlin in-process and exits before `native-image` starts.
- The builder's heap, code cache and metaspace are capped.
- `kotlin-reflect` (pulled in by Ktor, unused) is excluded, which halves the code native-image analyses.

I checked this in CI by running `install.sh` → `build.sh` → `test/run.sh` in an `ubuntu:24.04` container limited to 1 CPU, 1700 MB and no swap. It passed with the builder peaking at 1.42 GiB RSS.

## What's in it

- **Native image:** no JIT warm-up, and low memory left free for SQLite's page cache and connections.
- **Connection pool:** its own coroutine pool (a `Channel`) of 10 SQLite connections. Waiting for a connection suspends instead of blocking a thread.
  - Each connection prepares every query once and reuses it. That caches the plan, not data (rule 5).
- **SQLite pragmas:** WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`, `busy_timeout=5000`, mmap, a larger page cache and in-memory temp store, each run as its own statement.
  - Every write is committed before the 201 (rule 6).
- **JWT:** HS256 verified with `javax.crypto` and kotlinx.serialization.
  - Checks a constant-time signature, `alg`, `exp`, `nbf` and `iat`.
  - Every request is verified; nothing is cached.
- **SQL:** queries follow the reference shapes. Likes are one `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE EXISTS ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, plus an existence check only when nothing was inserted.
- **Logging:** INFO level via slf4j-simple, with nothing logged per request.

## Testing

- **This branch:** `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 on Ubuntu 24.04 in this repo's CI workflow, run on my own copy of the repo.
- **2 GB container check:** passed 42/42, as described above.
- **Load:** a local run of `bench/load.js` at 10,000 VUs passed. The server was pinned to one core, k6 ran on the same Windows machine, and the server was direct, without Nginx. Results: 0 failed requests out of about 183k, p95 77–91 ms, p99 235–284 ms. That's just a sanity check, not a prediction of the droplet result.

## Credits

This is based on @syorito-hatsuki's Kotlin + Ktor JVM submission (#36): routes, SQL and README structure. I ported it to a GraalVM native image and replaced HikariCP and java-jwt with the connection pool and JWT verification above.

title: AmmarServer C Submission
body:
Plain C on [AmmarServer](https://github.com/AmmarkoV/AmmarServer), my own HTTP server, with SQLite
compiled in from the amalgamation. **No Nginx** — it serves `0.0.0.0:80` itself.

| | |
|---|---|
| Language | C ( C11, gcc 13, `-O2` ) |
| HTTP server | AmmarServer, pinned by commit in `build.sh` |
| SQLite | 3.53.0, built from the official amalgamation ( pinned URL + sha256 ), not the apt package |
| Crypto | OpenSSL `libcrypto` for HS256 |
| Nginx or direct | **Direct**, `0.0.0.0:80` |
| Threads | **3**, at any load: one event loop serving every connection, one acceptor, one idle `main` |
 
`submissions/c-ammarserver-AmmarkoV/README.md` has the full reasoning and the optimisation list.

## Expected performance

Measured on my own machine, where k6 shares the CPU with the server, so these are ratios rather than
scores:

| | |
|---|---|
| `GET /feed`, existing keep-alive connection | avg **54 µs** idle, **65 µs** with 15,000 connections open, **74 µs** with 70,000 open |
| **70,000** idle keep-alive connections | 3 threads, **10.4 MB RSS**, **0 CPU ticks over a 60 s hold**; opened in 4.0 s, all 70,000 answered byte-correct |
| `POST /posts` sustained, one connection | **5,031 writes/s**, p50 96 µs, p99 212 µs |
| k6 `load.js`, 2,000 VUs | p95 **300 µs**, p99 **401 µs**, 0.00% errors, 27,064/27,064 checks |
| k6 `load.js`, 10,000 VUs | p95 **293 µs**, p99 **4.7 ms**, 0.00% errors, 183,547/183,547 checks, ~6% of one core |
| Kernel memory | ~3 KB of unreclaimable slab per connection, so ~200 MB at 65,000 |

**What I expect on the droplet.** At 10,000 VUs the whole load cost ~6% of one core here, i.e. ~72 µs
of CPU per request. Assuming a shared droplet vCPU is 2.5–3.5x slower per request ( this is the one
number I am guessing at ), that is ~180–250 µs, and at ~0.083 req/s per VU the CPU saturates somewhere
around **48,000–67,000 VUs**.

That happens to land on top of the other ceiling. Serving direct means one descriptor per connected
user, so `LimitNOFILE=65535` (See limitations underneath) caps this at **~65,527 connections** whatever the CPU can do. The two
independent limits coincide, so I would expect the limit-finding run to fail on CPU saturation or
descriptor exhaustion rather than on latency — p95 has three orders of magnitude of headroom against
the 500 ms threshold, so latency creep is not what should end it.

**The load generator may well bind first.** A connection is identified by its
`(source ip, source port, dest ip, dest port)` tuple, so one k6 address reaching one `ip:port` can open
at most as many connections as it has ephemeral ports. On a stock `ip_local_port_range`
( `32768 60999` ) I measured **28,230 connections from one source address, then `EADDRINUSE`** — under
half of what this serves. Worth checking `ip_local_port_range` on the k6 box, and whether it has more
than one address, before reading a failure above ~28,000 VUs as the server's.


## Limitations

- **Hard stop at ~65,527 connections, which is `LimitNOFILE=65535` and nothing else.** Spelling out
  how that number becomes the ceiling, since serving direct is what makes it binding:

  `LimitNOFILE` is the systemd directive that sets `RLIMIT_NOFILE` on the service — the most file
  descriptors the process may hold open at once, the same number `ulimit -n` reports. On Unix a socket
  *is* a descriptor, so **one connected user costs exactly one**, and this single number is the entire
  connection budget. It has a soft limit ( enforced now, and a process may raise its own freely ) and a
  hard limit ( the ceiling on the soft one, raising which needs `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE` ). `LimitNOFILE=65535`
  sets **both** to 65535, so there is no headroom to raise into, and rule 11 puts the unit file
  off-limits anyway. Subtract the handful this process needs for itself — the listening socket, the
  epoll instance, the database plus its `-wal` and `-shm`, and stdio — and the budget is ~65,527
  concurrent users.

  That is a wall, not a slope: `accept()` simply returns `EMFILE` and nothing further gets in, however
  idle the CPU is. So the failure above it is new connections being refused, not existing ones slowing
  down — which is why that path backs off rather than spins ( see Testing ).

  The soft/hard split is also worth watching when reproducing this outside systemd: a login shell
  typically gives soft 1024 against a hard limit of 1048576, so a server that never calls `setrlimit`
  quietly caps at **1024 connections** with a million descriptors unused, and says nothing — it just
  starts returning `EMFILE`. This process therefore raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at
  startup and prints the result, so the ceiling it is actually working with is on the record in its own
  output ( `descriptor limit 65535` on the benchmark box ).

  Exceeding 65,535 would need several processes behind `SO_REUSEPORT`, since each gets its own budget
  ( rule 1 allows any number of processes ). I did not, because the client side above runs out first
  and a second SQLite writer would cost WAL contention for a ceiling nothing can reach.
- **One thread means one slow operation delays everything, and the WAL checkpoint is that operation.**
  Over 20,000 sustained writes, 8 requests ( 0.04% ) took 16–94 ms against a 96 µs median; those are
  SQLite's auto-checkpoints fsyncing on the event loop thread. That was at 5,031 writes/s, about 56x
  the benchmark's real write rate, so expect them proportionally rarer — but the droplet's disk is
  likely slower than mine, so expect each to cost more. It is the single biggest contributor to the
  tail. Against a 1 s p99 budget there is room, and I left `wal_autocheckpoint` at its default rather
  than trade rare large stalls for frequent smaller ones, which is the worse shape for a p99.
- **Cold page cache at startup.** `/health` answers as soon as `SELECT 1` works, which can be before
  the 238 MB database is in the page cache; `GET /posts/:id` picks ids from across all 500,000 posts,
  so the early requests do real disk reads. The scored run's 2 minute warm-up covers this, but a
  benchmark started without one would see a slow first minute.
- **This design would not use a second core** if the box ever had one. It is deliberately single
  threaded for 1 vCPU.
- **`build.sh` needs the network**: it fetches AmmarServer from GitHub at a pinned commit and the
  SQLite amalgamation from sqlite.org at a pinned URL verified by sha256. No prebuilt binaries are
  committed or linked ( it links the three static archives it just built by full path, so a stale
  `libAmmarServer.so` cannot be picked up instead ).
- **Built `-march=native -mtune=native`**, so the binary is only valid on the host that built it — if
  the instruction set underneath it ever changed, that would be a `SIGILL` rather than a slow server.
  Everything is compiled from source on the box that runs it, so this is a tuned build rather than a
  portable one. For what it is worth, I could not measure it helping: `GET /feed` took 24.3 / 24.7 /
  25.4 µs without it and 24.2 / 24.7 / 25.0 µs with it, inside the noise, since SQLite's hot path is
  pointer chasing rather than arithmetic. It may do better on your core than on mine.
- **Requests are capped at 32 KB** and answered `413` beyond that. The spec puts bodies over 16 KB out
  of scope.
- **Responses carry no `Date` or `Server` header** — only `Content-Type`, `Content-Length` and
  `Connection`. HTTP/1.1 says a server SHOULD send `Date`; nothing in the test suite or the load test
  reads it, and there is no Nginx in front to add one. Compression is not implemented ( optional per
  the spec ).
- **Methods other than GET and POST on a known path return `404 not found`**, and percent-escapes in
  paths are not decoded. Both are out of scope per the spec.

## Rule notes

- **Rule 5** — every response is built from a SQLite read taken while the request is served, and every
  token's HMAC is recomputed from scratch. The only things reused across requests are prepared
  statements ( query plans, explicitly allowed ) and the two buffers the event loop reads and writes
  through.
- **Rule 6** — WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`. `INSERT ... RETURNING` is stepped all the way to
  `SQLITE_DONE` before the 201 is written, because with `RETURNING` it is that, not the first row,
  that ends the implicit transaction. No group commit: at ~90 writes/s it would save a fraction of a
  percent and risks exactly this rule.
- **Rule 3** — schema untouched. Foreign keys are left off ( SQLite's default ), so whether a post
  exists is asked outright before inserting a like; otherwise a like on a post that never existed
  would insert happily and answer 201 instead of 404.
- **Rule 11** — nothing on the box tuned: no kernel parameters, no CPU pinning, no `nice`. The only
  limit raised is this process's own descriptor soft limit, within the hard limit it was given. An
  explicit config path is passed to AmmarServer so its automatic lookup cannot pick up a stray
  `ammarServer.conf` and change the port or thread settings underneath the benchmark.

## Testing

- `test/test.sh` — **42/42**, from a clean build.
- 10 further framing checks of my own: pipelined requests in one write, a request dribbled out a byte
  at a time, a POST body arriving in a later segment, `Connection: close`, HTTP/1.0, bare-LF headers,
  an oversized request, an abandoned partial request, and an unknown method.
- Descriptor exhaustion: a server run at `ulimit -n 2048` and given 3,000 connections stayed at **1 CPU
  tick over 10 s** while saturated, and kept serving the connections it had accepted. `accept()`
  returning `EMFILE` backs off 50 ms and logs at most one line a second, rather than spinning the
  accept loop against the connections still being served.

C submission on a AI-written io_uring loop, SQLite in-process.

  **Runs direct, without Nginx**: the server listens on `0.0.0.0:80` itself (rule 9). Please
  benchmark it with `HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=80`, not behind `bench/nginx.conf`.

  This is my `c-h2o-einhornimmond` submission (#39) with its HTTP side replaced. The database code,
  the JWT check, the JSON reader and writer, the writer thread and its group commit are the same
  files. h2o's epoll loop, and with it LibreSSL and zlib, are gone; an io_uring loop written on the
  system calls (no liburing) stands where they were.

  - One io_uring loop on one thread: multishot accept, multishot receive into provided buffers,
    one `io_uring_enter` per pass, so no system call per request.
  - Connections are direct descriptors in the ring's table, which is as large as `LimitNOFILE`:
    the server holds 65,535 connections. Beyond that, new users wait in the backlog.
  - Reads run on the loop thread on a read-only SQLite connection. Writes go to one writer thread
    with group commit, and each response waits for its commit (WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`). The
    loop never waits for the disk.
  - No caching between requests; every token's signature is verified on every request. The schema
    is unchanged.
  - Needs Linux 6.1 or later (`DEFER_TASKRUN`); Ubuntu 24.04 has 6.8.

  Not measured on a droplet. On a development machine (Ryzen 7 5700G, kernel 6.1), in a container
  with one core, 2 GB and `nofile=65535`, load over loopback from the load generator of

body:
Adds `submissions/go-fasthttp-b3nhard/` — one folder, source only (no build output).

**Stack:** Go 1.27 + `valyala/fasthttp` v1.75, serving **directly on `0.0.0.0:80`** (no Nginx). SQLite access is via hand-written cgo bindings to `libsqlite3` — no `database/sql`.

**Optimizations**
- Allocation-free request handling: hand-written JSON scanner/encoder and a pooled scratch buffer for JWT decoding; reads allocate nothing, writes allocate a couple of bytes.
- No per-request read deadlines (`IdleTimeout`/`ReadTimeout` unset) — idle connections are simply never timed out, which satisfies SPEC's >=65 s requirement while removing a timer arm/cancel per request.
- `ReduceMemoryUsage`, 1 GiB `mmap_size`, prepared statements per connection.
- WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`; every write is stepped to `SQLITE_DONE` before responding.
- `PASSIVE` WAL checkpoints run on a dedicated connection so maintenance never sits in a request's path.
- GC effectively off (`SetGCPercent(-1)`) behind a 512 MiB soft `GOMEMLIMIT`.

**Measured locally:** ~135 MiB peak RSS with 15,000 concurrent connections, 0 errors, p95 ~0.7 ms / p99 ~3.6 ms.

**Tests:** `bash test/run.sh submissions/go-fasthttp-b3nhard` passes all 42 checks. Dependency versions are pinned in `go.mod`/`go.sum`.

title: Add java-netty-itsnaveenk submission
body:
### Summary
This PR adds a high-performance **Java 21 + Netty** submission designed for maximum throughput and concurrency on the $12 droplet (1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM).

### Stack & Architecture
- **Language**: Java 21 LTS (`openjdk-21-jdk-headless`)
- **Framework**: Raw Netty 4.1.118.Final with native Linux Epoll (`EpollServerSocketChannel`)
- **Database**: SQLite 3.45.1 in WAL mode (`org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` 3.45.1.0)
- **JSON**: Custom zero-allocation streaming `ByteBuf` byte serializer (`FastJsonWriter`)
- **Mode**: **Direct** on `0.0.0.0:80` (avoids 15–20% Nginx single-core CPU overhead and bypasses Nginx connection limits)

### Key Optimizations
1. **Direct ResultSet-to-ByteBuf Streaming**: On `/feed` (46% of traffic) and `/posts/:id` (46% of traffic), row data is streamed directly from the native SQLite `ResultSet` into Netty's pre-sized `ByteBuf`, completely eliminating domain record objects (`List<Post>`, `Post`), intermediate strings, and GC churn.
2. **Batched Socket Flushes via `channelReadComplete()`**: Instead of issuing an immediate `writeAndFlush` system call on every request, responses are queued with `ctx.write()` and flushed in batches during Netty's `channelReadComplete(ctx)` hook, coalescing writes into a single `writev()` system call.
3. **Single Epoll EventLoop with Inline Non-Blocking Writes**: On 1 vCPU, multi-threaded worker pools or background write threads force costly OS thread context switches (20–50 $\mu s$ per switch). In SQLite WAL mode with `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL`, commits do not fsync and complete in under 35 $\mu s$. Running writes inline eliminates thread hops, queue mutexes, and `CompletableFuture` allocations entirely.
4. **Dedicated Read vs. Write Connections**: Readers and writers run on independent connection handles in WAL mode with 1 GiB memory mapping (`mmap_size = 1073741824`) and `query_only = 1` on readers.
5. **Zero-Allocation Custom JSON Serializer (`FastJsonWriter`)**:
   - Long digits formatted using a thread-local buffer (no `byte[]` heap allocation).
   - Strings written using Netty's 4-argument `ByteBufUtil.writeUtf8(buf, str, start, end)` to prevent `subSequence` substring allocations.
   - ISO-8601 timestamps and usernames written directly as quoted ASCII without escape scanning.
6. **Zero-Copy Path and ID Parsing**: `StringUtil.parsePositiveId(CharSequence seq, int start, int end)` parses route parameters directly from the URI string into primitive `long`s without substring allocations or `java.lang.Long` heap boxing.
7. **Fast HMAC-SHA256 JWT Verification**: Reuses pre-initialized `ThreadLocal<Mac>` instances with in-place ASCII byte copying and constant-time signature comparisons. Common standard headers (`{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}`) are fast-path matched to bypass base64 decoding.
8. **Kernel Socket Options & Buffer Tuning**:
   - `SO_RCVBUF = 4096`
   - `SO_SNDBUF = 16384` (ensures full feed responses fit in a single TCP send window without epoll wait cycles)
   - `TCP_NODELAY = true`
   - `TCP_QUICKACK = true` (disables delayed ACKs to minimize round-trip latency)
   - `SO_BACKLOG = 8192`
9. **Serial Garbage Collector & JVM Tuning**: Configured with `-XX:+UseSerialGC -Xms512m -Xmx512m -Xmn384m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` to eliminate background GC threads, fix heap boundaries, pre-fault memory pages, and keep young gen collections virtually non-existent. Netty bounds checks and accessibility validations in hot loops are disabled via `-Dio.netty.buffer.checkBounds=false -Dio.netty.buffer.checkAccessible=false`.

### Test Verification
Passed all 42 checks in `test/test.sh` via `test/run.sh`:
```text
passed=42 failed=0
```

title: Bun + Elysia submission (`submissions/bun-elysia-shashishsoni/`).
body:
# Bun + Elysia submission

Adds `submissions/bun-elysia-shashishsoni/`: the feed API on Bun with Elysia, tuned for the $12 box (1 vCPU, 2 GB).

## Stack

| Component | Choice |
|---|---|
| Runtime | Bun 1.3.14 (pinned, installed from the official release tarball) |
| Framework | Elysia 1.4.30 (pinned via `bun.lock`), lean mode: `aot: true`, `normalize: false`, no schemas, no plugins |
| SQLite driver | Built-in `bun:sqlite`: one request connection with reused prepared statements, plus one checkpoint connection on a worker thread |
| JSON | Native `JSON.stringify` with SPEC-ordered object literals |
| Mode | **Direct**: `HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=80`, `idleTimeout: 30s`. (With a loopback `HOST`, i.e. behind Nginx / in CI, it uses `idleTimeout: 70s` so Nginx's 64 upstream keepalives are never closed early.) |

## Optimizations, and why

- **Direct instead of Nginx.** The bench Nginx runs one worker with `worker_connections 16384`, so it can't hold more than ~16k users' keep-alive connections no matter how fast the app is.
- **30 s idle timeout (direct mode).** Every user holds its own socket, so at 80k+ users the server is always near the 65,535-descriptor cap. Bun sweeps idle sockets every 4 s, so `idleTimeout: 30` really closes after 28–32 s (measured) — far above every think gap (3–15 s, including the ≤ 8 s pauses before a like/post, so a POST never races the server's close; only idempotent GETs are retried). Eviction itself is left to the proportional shedder below, which closes finished responses smoothly; the sweep then only reaps strays instead of firing synchronized 4 s-quantum herds. Measured at 80k users: with the previous 13 s timeout the sweep owned eviction and gave p95 2.1 s with ~30K accept-queue overflows per run; with 30 s it gives p95 0.23 s with ~2K, then zero. (With a 10 s timeout, really 8–12 s, POSTs raced the close and pushed p99 over 1 s at 60k users.)
- **Proportional shedding under descriptor pressure.** Past ~56k users the descriptor limit binds; then `accept()` can't take new users and they sit in the kernel queue until they time out. Every 50 ms the server checks its open-descriptor count (`statSync('/proc/self/fd').size`, O(1) on Linux ≥ 6.2, ~1 µs) against `/proc/self/limits`, and sheds a fraction of finished responses that ramps 0 → 100% between 85% and 95% of the limit — closing right after answering, never mid-request. The previous all-or-nothing flag (shed everything above 92%) evicted in synchronized herds whose reconnect bursts overflowed Bun's fixed 512-entry accept queue (~30K dropped SYNs per 80k run, each costing 1–3 s); proportional shedding cut that to 58 failed requests and p95 1.3 s before the idle-timeout change above.
- **WAL checkpoints on a worker thread.** With SQLite's auto-checkpoint, the commit that crosses the threshold copies pages into the DB and `fsync`s on the event-loop thread. Any event-loop stall risks overflowing the 512-entry accept backlog. The request connection sets `wal_autocheckpoint=0`; a `Worker` with its own connection runs `wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` every second. If the worker ever dies, auto-checkpoint is switched back on.
- **One request connection.** On 1 vCPU a pool only adds context switches and `SQLITE_BUSY` retries. Prepared statements cache the query plan (allowed by rule 5); every request still reads fresh data from SQLite.
- **Feed walks the index, then counts.** `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20` scans `posts_created_at_id_idx` and stops after 20 rows, with one covering-index `count(*)` per post (~25 µs). A `LEFT JOIN likes ... GROUP BY p.id` looks equivalent but aggregates all 500k posts before the `LIMIT` (~770 ms).
- **Lean Elysia.** No `t` schemas, no plugins, no OpenAPI. Handlers validate manually and return a raw `Response` with compact JSON, which skips validation overhead and preserves exact key order. Measured overhead against plain `Bun.serve` with identical handlers: ~12% CPU.
- **Hot-path parsing without `BigInt`.** `parsePostId`/`sub` validation used `BigInt`, which allocates per request. `parsePostId` now strips leading zeros and compares against `"9007199254740991"` as a string (length > 16 can only be a 404 sentinel); `sub` just checks digits plus a nonzero digit. Same 400/404/401 behavior, no bigint allocation.
- **JWT header fast path.** Seed and test tokens all use the fixed header `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}`, so matching headers skip a base64 decode + `JSON.parse`; anything else falls back to full parse plus the HS256 check. Signature (`node:crypto` HMAC + `timingSafeEqual`), `exp`/`nbf`, `sub`/`username` shape still verified on every request — no verification caching (rule 5).
- **Hand-verified HS256 JWT** as above (algorithm pinned, no library overhead).
- **Single-statement likes** (`INSERT ... SELECT WHERE EXISTS ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`). The existence check runs only when nothing was inserted, which distinguishes `already_liked` from `post not found` without an extra read on the hot path.
- **Inserts use `RETURNING id, created_at`.** No JS clock and no timestamp-format drift; autocommit commits before the 201 is sent (rule 6).
- **Pragmas:** `WAL`, `synchronous=NORMAL`, `busy_timeout=5000`, `mmap_size=512MB`, `cache_size=64MB`, `temp_store=MEMORY`, `journal_size_limit=64MB`.
- **Clean layers** (`config` / `db` / `checkpoint` / `connections` / `auth` / `validation` / `http` / `index`), each function small and single-purpose, with `bun:test` unit tests for auth, validation and the shed curve.

## Verified

- **`test/test.sh`: passed=42 failed=0** in both modes (`HOST=127.0.0.1` as CI runs it, and `HOST=0.0.0.0` as benchmarked), each on a fresh seed copy. `bun test`: 15/15.
- **k6 load test with `bench/load.js`** (official tool). The server ran limited like the droplet: `systemd-run --scope -p AllowedCPUs=0 -p MemoryMax=2G -p MemoryMin=2G` plus `prlimit --nofile=65535`, direct on `:80`, on a fresh DB copy each run. k6 ran on the same machine (Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL2) and was kept off the server's core. `MemoryMin` only stops k6's memory use from evicting the server's pages; the server is still capped at 2 GB. The load was split across 4 k6 instances, each on its own loopback source IP (one source IP only has ~28k ephemeral ports), started paused and released together. Measured before the shedding/idle changes above:

  | VUs | Hold | Result | p95 | p99 | Errors |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 50,000 | 5 min | ✅ pass | 3.2 ms | 79 ms | 0.000% |
  | 60,000 | 5 min | ✅ pass | 17 ms | 123 ms | 0.000% |
  | 65,000 | 5 min | ✅ pass | 48 ms | 176 ms | 0.000% |
  | 70,000 | 5 min | ✅ pass | 60 ms | 839 ms | 0.000% |
  | **75,000** | **5 min** | ✅ **pass (k6 max)** | **212 ms** | **578 ms** | **0.000%** (2.79M requests) |
  | 77,500 | 2 min | ❌ fail | 1.19 s | 3.6 s | 0.012% |
  | 80,000 | 2 min | ❌ fail | 4.8 s | 11.5 s | 0.25% |

- **Raw-socket harness past k6's limit.** k6 tops out around 10–30k VUs per machine (a JS runtime per VU: 4 × 20k VUs stalled during init), so higher levels used a purpose-built generator: 1 TCP connection per user, the same request mix / probabilities / think times as `load.js`, k6's rules (60 s timeout = error, GET retried once on a stale connection, POST not retried), calibrated against k6 within ~2x at 2k users. Same limits as above (1 pinned CPU, 65535 files, direct `:8080`), 60 s ramp + 90 s holds:

  | Users | Reqs | p50 | p95 | p99 | Errors | Server core |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 80,000 | 1.08M | 0.25 ms | 3.8 ms | 45 ms | 0 | ~45% |
  | 100,000 | 1.36M | 0.25 ms | 0.82 ms | 3.8 ms | 0 | ~55% |
  | 120,000 | 1.63M | 0.28 ms | 1.5 ms | 10 ms | 0 | ~62% |
  | 150,000 | 2.03M | 0.48 ms | 18 ms | 40 ms | 0 | ~73% |
  | 180,000 | 2.38M | 45 ms | 304 ms | 570 ms | 0 | ~81% |
  | 200,000 | 2.51M ×2 | ~200 ms | 513 / 518 ms | 734 / 1007 ms | 0–2 | ~84% |

  Clean passes through **180,000 users**; 200,000 fails p95 (and p99 on the rerun) as the core saturates and accept-queue drops return. Server FDs pin at ~57–60K throughout (the shedder holding its equilibrium); WAL residue stays under its 64 MB cap; no run ever ran short of memory.
- **What the harness runs showed.** Request CPU was never the wall: at 80k the core sat at ~27% while p95 blew out — the failures were connection churn at the FD cap, not request serving. Three changes moved the wall from ~75k to ~180k: proportional instead of binary shedding (80k: 432 → 58 fails, p95 2.1 s → 1.3 s), idle 13 s → 30 s so smooth shedding instead of sweep herds owns eviction (p95 → 0.23 s, drops → ~0), plus the parsing fast-paths. The ceiling now is plain core saturation plus accept-queue drops at ~60k pinned FDs.
- **Caveat:** the local core is faster than the droplet's shared vCPU, the harness is not k6, and holds were 90 s rather than 5 min — so expect the real score to land below the local numbers. The k6-verified max remains 75,000 pending a droplet re-run of the current code.
- **Repo hygiene:** source only (`node_modules/` ignored, `bun.lock` committed). A folder-level `.gitattributes` forces LF on the shell scripts. No files are touched outside the submission folder.

title: Add C# NativeAOT io_uring submission with asynchronous SQLite writes
body:
Add a direct C# HTTP/1.1 implementation that keeps the socket loop responsive while SQLite writes and checkpoints wait for disk I/O. Reads use prepared SQL-generated UTF-8 JSON and SQLite mmap; a separate writer groups requests and releases their responses only after COMMIT.

The application uses .NET 10 NativeAOT and a small source-built liburing byte-transport bridge. Six registered-file tables avoid the ordinary 65,535-descriptor ceiling without changing RLIMIT or kernel settings. HTTP parsing, routing, JWT validation and SQLite access are C#. SQLite 3.53.4 is SHA-256 pinned and built with a synthetic build-time PGO profile. The schema stays unchanged, foreign keys remain enabled, and there are no response, row or JWT-verification caches.

Validation:
- 42/42 official checks on Ubuntu 24.04, built from source on a 1 vCPU / 2 GiB Azure Spot VM.
- Regression checks for Unicode/NUL, empty and tied feeds, live external SQLite updates, duplicate likes, FK failures, malformed JWTs, reads during a blocked writer and SIGKILL/restart after 64 acknowledged writes.
- Transport checks for byte fragmentation, chunked UTF-8 with trailers, 100 Continue, ordered pipelined writes, output backpressure and abandoned uploads.

Final k6 confirmation: unmodified bench/load.js, k6 2.3.0, 1,000-user two-minute warm-up, 10,000 users with 60 s ramp / 300 s hold / 30 s ramp-down, default client GC and original host settings. 373,460 requests, zero errors, p95 0.416 ms / p99 1.34 ms. This is a passing point, not a searched maximum or an official score.

Diagnostic capacity result: 150,000 users, 60 s ramp and 5-minute hold, raw-socket approximation of bench/load.js, hold p95 5.70 ms / p99 38.16 ms, zero hold failures. This is explicitly NOT an official score: private benchmark traffic bypassed Azure guest connection tracking, and the generator was not k6. Those fixture changes are absent from the submission. The initial 300,000-user prototype was OOM-killed; memory-aware admission was added afterward. No first-place claim is made.

Credits: database/JWT/JSON work derives from maks-march's PR #27; SQL JSON/mmap experiments were informed by PRs #13 and #9, and registered-file/group-commit techniques by raoz's PR #26 and hendy643's PR #32. The new folder retains these references and the repository's MIT licensing.
