title: add node + fastify
body:
# Node + Fastify

Tokens are verified in `auth.ts` with `node:crypto`: one HMAC per request,
constant-time signature compare, `exp`/`nbf` checked every time. Everything
else is tuned around that core — SQLite BLOB bodies, pragmas, keep-alive
tuning.

|                     |                                                                                    |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Language            | TypeScript 7.0.2, compiled to ESM for Node.js 24.21.0 (official linux-x64 tarball) |
| Framework           | Fastify 5.12.7                                                                     |
| SQLite driver       | better-sqlite3 13.0.3 (synchronous, compiled against Ubuntu's SQLite)              |
| Types               | `@types/node` 24.19.2, `@types/better-sqlite3` 9.6.0 (dev only)                    |
| **Nginx or direct** | **Direct**: serves `0.0.0.0:80` itself                                             |

All dependency versions are pinned in `package.json` + `package-lock.json`.

## Layout

```
src/
  server.ts    # entrypoint: builds the app and listens on HOST:PORT
  app.ts       # Fastify instance, parsers, error handlers, all five routes
  db.ts        # the single SQLite connection, pragmas, prepared statements
             # (reads/creates return whole response bodies as Buffers)
  auth.ts      # HS256 verification (header fast path, one HMAC per request,
             # constant-time compare; every request, nothing cached)
  ids.ts       # post-id validation
  config.ts    # SQLITE_PATH, JWT_SECRET, HOST, PORT from the environment
  responses.ts # compact-JSON helpers for errors, health and likes
             # (post/feed bodies come straight from SQLite, no JS serialization)
```

`tsconfig.json` uses `strict` plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`,
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`,
`useUnknownInCatchVariables` and `noEmitOnError`, so `build.sh` fails rather
than shipping a type error. One deliberate addition to the base options is
`esModuleInterop` (emit-neutral for ESM output): Fastify's and
`@types/better-sqlite3`'s typings use `export =`, which TypeScript cannot
default-import under `module: ESNext` without it.

## Running it

```bash
sudo bash install.sh   # Node 24.21.0 + build-essential, python3, curl
bash build.sh          # npm ci, then tsc -p tsconfig.json (src/ -> dist/)
SQLITE_PATH=... JWT_SECRET=... HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=80 bash start.sh
```

## Optimizations, and why

- **One process, sync SQLite calls inline on the event loop.** The box has one vCPU, so worker processes or a threadpool would only add context switches. Every query is an index or primary-key lookup finishing in well under a millisecond. One connection also means writes never wait on SQLite locks, so no `SQLITE_BUSY` retries.
- **Direct instead of Nginx.** On one core, Nginx's CPU comes straight out of Node's budget, and p99 < 1 s is the limit that fails first near saturation. Node's HTTP server holds ~15k idle keep-alive connections cheaply. `keepAliveTimeout` is 75 s (SPEC wants >= 65 s behind Nginx; direct clients also reuse long-lived keep-alives) with `headersTimeout` 80 s set on the underlying HTTP server (Fastify v5 exposes no such option) and `backlog` 4096 on `listen`, as Node requires `headersTimeout > keepAliveTimeout`.
- **Lean Fastify setup.** No schema validation, no logger, no global auth hook (GETs pay zero JWT cost). A single raw-buffer JSON content parser feeds `POST /posts` (plus a `'*'` fallback so exotic content types map to the SPEC's `malformed JSON body` instead of Fastify's 415), which parses with `JSON.parse` once. Like responses are template-built `Buffer`s (`post_id` is a validated integer, so interpolation is exact); errors stay `JSON.stringify`'d small literals on cold paths.
- **Whole response bodies come from SQLite as BLOBs.** The feed is one `group_concat` of per-row `json_object(...)` fragments with the `{"posts":[ ... ]}` envelope concatenated in SQL; single posts and `INSERT ... RETURNING` likewise return the full `{"post":...}` body. Statements are `.pluck()`ed, so better-sqlite3 hands handlers a `Buffer` that Fastify sends without decoding to string or re-encoding — no per-row object allocation, no JS string building, no serializer on the hot paths. Key order follows the `json_object()` argument order and escaping matches `JSON.stringify` byte-for-byte (verified against the golden files). No response caching anywhere: every request reads SQLite while being served (rule 5).
- **HS256 JWT verification.** One `crypto.createHmac` per request, constant-time signature compare, `exp`/`nbf` checked — every token verified on every request (rule 5: no remembered verifications). A prefix fast path skips the header parse for the standard `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}` header, which is what all seed and test tokens use; anything else goes through a full HS256-only header check. `auth.ts` preserves the SPEC's exact error split (`missing bearer token` / `invalid or expired token` / `invalid token payload`, auth before id).
- **SQL**: the reference queries. Each like is a single statement, `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE EXISTS (post) ON CONFLICT (user_id, post_id) DO NOTHING` (anonymous placeholders bound positionally — better-sqlite3 counts each `?NNN` occurrence separately, so `?1`/`?2` numbering throws); a post-existence check runs only when it inserted nothing, to tell "already liked" from "no such post". Prepared statements are reused (plan cache, not data cache).
- **Pragmas**: `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` (single process: the file lock is taken once, not per statement), `journal_mode=WAL`, `synchronous=NORMAL` (rule 6), `foreign_keys=OFF` (better-sqlite3 enforces FKs by default — verified on a fresh db — so this skips a PK probe per insert and matches the reference implementations), 1 GiB `mmap_size`, 64 MiB page cache, `temp_store=MEMORY`, `journal_size_limit` 64 MiB, `wal_autocheckpoint` 10k pages (fewer event-loop-blocking fsync batches under writes; durability is unaffected). No `busy_timeout`: with one connection in exclusive mode it can never fire. Writes run in autocommit, so each 201 is committed before the response.
- **Body validation** uses native `String.prototype.trim()` (exactly the SPEC's trim set) and codepoint length (`[...s].length`) for the 500-character limit.

## License

MIT, under the repo's [license](../../LICENSE).

title: Add c-epoll-TheFirstIstari submission (C, raw epoll, SQLite; direct on :80)
body:
## C + raw epoll + SQLite, served direct

Single-threaded C11 HTTP/1.1 on edge-triggered epoll (~2,100 lines, no framework, no third-party code). SQLite 3.53.x amalgamation (pinned, SHA-256 verified, PGO+LTO). Hand-rolled SHA-256/HMAC/JWT/JSON/HTTP. Serves direct on `$HOST:$PORT`.

**The idea:** the think-time workload is bound by concurrent idle connections, not req/s, so the FD ceiling (`LimitNOFILE=65535`) is the score ceiling. This server escapes it with **pressure-based eviction of idle keep-alives** (drains + `Connection: close` past ~60k fds, hysteresis release at ~55k, clients reconnect transparently) — no response/query caching, every request reads live SQLite, JWT verified per request.

Plus: group commit (no response before COMMIT; commit/rollback failure converts the batch to 500s), idle conns hold no buffers, timing-wheel timeouts, WAL+NORMAL+EXCLUSIVE, 1 GiB mmap, passive WAL checkpoints, trimmed + PGO SQLite build.

**Validation (all on the PR code):**
- `test/run.sh` path (install.sh + PGO build + start.sh + test.sh) in a droplet-limits container: **42/42**
- 39 API-level checks incl. byte-exact `test/golden/` comparisons; ~50 unit checks (oracle-verified crypto vectors); ASan/UBSan clean
- SIGKILL mid-load: 300/300 acknowledged creates survive restart; FK violations return 500 (never phantom 201)
- Capacity (official `bench/load.js`, CachyOS x86_64, 1-CPU/2 GB/no-swap container, k6 on other cores): **70,000 users 5-min hold PASS** (2.61M checks, 0 failed, p95 ~113µs, p99 ~5.6ms); **85,000 users 2-min PASS**; saturation ~107k req/s
- Same-box head-to-head: champion C/io_uring also passes 70k/5-min (p95 ~5ms, p99 ~10.6ms); saturation Rust/epoll ~107k, C/io_uring ~94k, C++/uWS ~83k, C/epoll ~81k, Zig ~80k, C/fio ~67k (all 42/42)

Details, methodology, and reproduction scripts are in the submission README + `dev/`.

title: Add go-epoll-Antheurus submission (Go, raw epoll, SQLite, direct)
body:
Adds `submissions/go-epoll-Antheurus/`: Go with no framework, serving port 80 directly.

| | |
|---|---|
| Language | Go 1.27.2 |
| HTTP | hand-written HTTP/1.1 on raw `epoll` syscalls, parsed from bytes |
| SQLite | 3.54.0 amalgamation compiled in via a small cgo shim (no `database/sql`) |
| JWT / JSON | hand-written HS256 and a strict JSON validator |
| Dependencies | Go standard library + SQLite only |
| Nginx or direct | **Direct** on `0.0.0.0:80` |

**How it works**

- HTTP/1.1 is parsed straight from bytes on a raw epoll loop, one thread per process. Each connection is a small struct in a table indexed by fd, not a goroutine, and the steady state allocates nothing, so the GC doesn't run under load.
- Each query is one cgo call that binds, steps every row and copies the columns out.
- Writes are queued during a loop pass and committed together in one short transaction at the end. Every response goes out only after its commit. `BEGIN` never waits: if another process holds the lock, the writes retry a millisecond later while reads keep being served.
- A checkpointer thread runs `RESTART` checkpoints. My first version used `PASSIVE`, and under a steady write load the WAL never rewound: it hit 800 MB in a minute.
- Every JWT is verified on every request.

**Why there are up to three processes**

`LimitNOFILE=65535` is per process, so one process can't hold much more than ~59k connections. Past that, k6 users start reconnecting. But each process that serves traffic adds CPU of its own, so plain `SO_REUSEPORT` hashing across several processes was slower. Instead, the first process attaches a one-instruction classic BPF program to the reuseport group (`SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_CBPF`). The program steers new connections to whichever process is currently filling up and moves on when it's full. So below ~56k users only one process does anything. If a process dies, it falls back to plain hashing and restarts it.

What the layout costs at the same load:

| Users | Layout | Server CPU |
|---:|---|---:|
| 55,000 | one process | 37–38 % |
| 55,000 | two processes, hashed | 45–47 % |
| 55,000 | steered (this PR) | 40 % |
| 80,000 | two processes, hashed | 53–55 % |
| 80,000 | three processes, hashed | 68 % |
| 120,000 | two processes, hashed | fail (fd limit hit, 19k reconnects) |
| 120,000 | steered (this PR) | 68 %, pass |

**Testing**

- `bash test/run.sh submissions/go-epoll-Antheurus`: 42/42 on a clean Ubuntu 24.04 linux/amd64 container (after `install.sh`) and on linux/arm64.
- `e2e_test.go` covers things curl in the suite doesn't: pipelining behind a write, requests split across packets, `Connection: close`, HTTP/1.0, `Expect: 100-continue`, chunked bodies (501).

Load numbers are local only: a Docker container limited to 1 CPU and 2 GB on an M2. k6 needs ~280 KB per user, so `loadgen/` replays `bench/load.js` over raw TCP with one keep-alive connection per user, scored the same way (p95 < 500 ms, p99 < 1 s, < 1% failed).

| Users | Hold | Failed | p95 | p99 | Server CPU | Result |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 55,000 | 90 s | 0 | 1.0 ms | 28 ms | 40 % | pass |
| 80,000 | 90 s | 0 | 1.4 ms | 229 ms | 57 % | pass |
| 120,000 | 120 s | 0 of 1.52M | 5.4 ms | 223 ms | 68 % | pass |
| 120,000 | 300 s | 0 of 3.81M | 1.0 ms | 14 ms | 64 % | pass |
| 120,000 | 300 s | 0 of 3.81M | 0.87 ms | 3.6 ms | 67 % | pass |
| 122,500 | 120 s | | | | 101 % | fail |
| 125,000 | 120 s | | | | 93 % | fail |

The two 300 s rows are the confirm step from the scoring (a five-minute hold), run twice in a row on the exact commit in this PR; every one of the 120,004 connections stayed open the whole time. Then the same commit on x86: a 6-vCPU AMD EPYC VPS (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8), server container again held to 1 CPU and 2 GB, load clients on the same machine:

| Users | Hold | Failed | p95 | p99 | Server CPU | Result |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 50,000 | 120 s | 0 | 33 ms | 199 ms | 79 % | pass |
| 55,000 | 300 s | 0 of 1.74M | 22 ms | 168 ms | 78 % | pass |
| 57,500 | 300 s | 0 | 374 ms | 1.13 s | 90 % | fail |
| 60,000 | 120 s | 0 | 2.0 s | 3.6 s | 94 % | fail |

So about 55k there; each request costs roughly twice the CPU it does on the M2. That box was also running other services, and with the load clients on the same kernel part of their receive work lands on the server's CPU, so I'd read it as a floor. My guess for the droplet is somewhere between the two. The README has the details and the things I tried and dropped.

body:
## Summary

A Kotlin + Spring Boot 4 submission that stays idiomatic, maintainable Spring (`@RestController` → service →
`JdbcClient` repository, `@RestControllerAdvice`, kotlinx.serialization data classes) and is tuned for one vCPU
with every optimization kept only if a load test showed it winning.

- **Stack:** Kotlin 2.3.21, Spring Boot 4.1.1 (Spring MVC, Tomcat 11, virtual threads), Oracle GraalVM for
  JDK 25.0.4 on the JVM (Graal JIT), sqlite-jdbc 3.53.2.1 + HikariCP, kotlinx.serialization (no Jackson).
- **Nginx or direct:** **Direct** (`0.0.0.0:80`).
- **Main optimizations:** no kotlin-reflect (Spring MVC then calls handlers with plain `Method.invoke`),
  per-connection reuse of compiled SQL statements, trimmed filter chain, small Tomcat per-connection buffers,
  Graal JIT + Serial GC + 1 GB heap + transparent huge pages, one reader pool + one writer connection.
- **Tried and rejected (with numbers in the README):** GraalVM native image (can't be built in 2 GB; ~15% more
  CPU/request than the warmed JIT), Jetty, C2, Parallel/G1 GC, platform threads, compact object headers,
  bigger heaps/young gen, group commit.

Did not really push to the full limits, I have work to do unfortunately but this my go at a more "real" maintainable version.  

## Local results

Docker, server container `--cpus=1 --memory=2g` running this `start.sh`, k6 `bench/load.js` in separate
containers, after a 2-minute warm-up at 1,000 users:

| Load | CPU/request | p95 | p99 | Errors | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30k users, 5-minute hold (~2,900 req/s) | 184 µs | 3.1 ms | 19 ms | 0% | 821 MiB |

No degradation over a 25-minute soak; 15,000 idle keep-alive connections cost ~104 MiB. The local core is faster
than a droplet vCPU, so treat the absolute numbers as optimistic.

## Checklist

- [x] `test/test.sh`: 42/42 in an `ubuntu:24.04` container (`--cpus=1 --memory=2g`) after `install.sh` + `build.sh`
- [x] Only files under `submissions/kotlin-springboot-Mindstorm1750/`
- [x] `install.sh` (root), `build.sh`, `start.sh` (foreground), `README.md`, `.gitignore`; no build output committed
- [x] Versions pinned (Gradle wrapper with checksum, Spring Boot BOM, GraalVM tarball sha256)
- [x] WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`, autocommit; no response/query/JWT caching (statement reuse caches plans only)
- [x] Healthy in ~5 s after `start.sh`

title: feat: Add Java-Quarkus-Wolches solution
body:
# Java + Quarkus submission (`submissions/java-quarkus-wolches`) 
### A standard Quarkus (JVM) service featuring a multitier architecture and a reactive approach. 
#### 65k users / 5.4k RPS

| | |
|--|--|
| Language / runtime | Java 25 (Temurin 25.0.3+9) |
| Framework | Quarkus 3.40.1: Quarkus REST on Vert.x, Jackson |
| SQLite | `quarkus-jdbc-sqlite` 3.0.11 over `sqlite-jdbc` 3.46.1.3 (bundled SQLite 3.46.1), Agroal |
| JWT | `quarkus-smallrye-jwt`, HS256 |
| Mode | **Direct**, `0.0.0.0:80` |

## What Quarkus gives out of the box

- **Build-time bootstrap.** CDI wiring, REST routing, Jackson (de)serializers and config are
  resolved when `build.sh` runs, not at startup. There is no classpath scanning or reflection
  at runtime; the JVM is healthy 1–2 s after `start.sh`.
- **Non-blocking HTTP** on Vert.x/Netty: one event loop per core, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, tens of
  thousands of idle connections cost memory, not threads.
- **Reflection-free Jackson**: serializers for the response records are generated at build time.
- **Fast-jar packaging** with its class-loading index, Agroal connection pooling, SmallRye JWT
  (jose4j) for signature and `exp` checks.

## Optimizations made on top, without hurting maintainability

- **Direct instead of Nginx.** On one core, Nginx's CPU comes straight out of the application's
  budget, and Vert.x handles the idle keep-alive connections itself.
- **Reactive endpoints, two dedicated database threads.** Every endpoint returns a Mutiny `Uni`.
  All SQL runs on two single-threaded Vert.x worker executors: one owns the writer connection,
  one owns a read-only reader connection. On one vCPU this is exactly the parallelism SQLite
  can use, with no pool contention and no lock waits in application code.
- **Separate read and write data sources** (standard Quarkus named datasources): reader opened
  with `open_mode=1`, writer with `foreign_keys=true`. Each pool holds one connection for the
  life of the process.
- **Per-connection prepared-statement cache**, the reference SQL from SPEC.md, result sets
  always closed, and one small `tx()` helper that commits or rolls back on every outcome, so a
  404 can never leave a read transaction open and pin the reader to a stale snapshot.
- **Likes are a single `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.** The update count tells "first like"
  from "already liked", and the foreign-key error for a missing post becomes the 404, so there
  is no existence query before or after the insert.
- **JVM sized for the box**: `-Xms512m -Xmx1g -XX:+UseSerialGC`. On a single core the concurrent
  collectors only add threads that compete with the event loop.

## Tests

`src/test` is a Java port of `test/test.sh` (same checks, same byte-exact golden comparisons)
plus a port of `seed/make-seed.sh` that rebuilds `seed/feed.db` with the published content
checksum, so `mvn test` is self-contained. `install.sh`, `build.sh`, `start.sh` and
`test/run.sh` were also run on a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container as CI does: 42/42 checks pass,
healthy 2 s after `start.sh`.

## Local load test

Not the benchmark box, so treat these as an order of magnitude: Docker Desktop on a Windows
ARM64 host, the app limited to `--cpus=1 --memory=2g` without swap and `nofile=65535`, k6 in
sibling containers (split over several containers above 30k VUs so the client never runs out
of ephemeral ports). `bench/load.js` as is, 60 s ramp, 2-minute holds while searching, a fresh
copy of `seed/feed.db` for every run.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2,500 | 21 ms | 70 ms | 0% | 207 | 10% | 307 MB | pass |
| 5,000 | 7.6 ms | 31 ms | 0% | 416 | 19% | 350 MB | pass |
| 10,000 | 2.3 ms | 3.8 ms | 0% | 833 | 28% | 372 MB | pass |
| 20,000 | 2.3 ms | 5.1 ms | 0% | 1,664 | 35% | 437 MB | pass |
| 40,000 | 10.6 ms | 63 ms | 0% | 3,325 | 50% | 683 MB | pass |

| 65,000 | 48 ms | 174 ms | 0% | 5,406 | 89% | 772 MB | pass |
| 65,500 | 221 ms | 1.64 s | 0.00% | 5,417 | 74% | 1.06 GB | fail |
| 66,250 | 1.19 s | 2.27 s | 0.12% | 5,386 | 68% | 1.35 GB | fail |

title: feat(c): add single-threaded C + io_uring submission (c-iouring-27bhd)
body:
## Summary

Adds `submissions/c-iouring-27bhd`, a zero-framework, single-threaded **C + `io_uring` + in-tree PGO SQLite** implementation serving `0.0.0.0:80` directly.

The initial C implementation encountered lock contention across 8 worker threads sharing a single SQLite write lock on a 1-vCPU instance. Because the challenge hardware provides 1 vCPU, this implementation eliminates thread pools and mutexes entirely, running the network event loop and sequential SQLite queries on **1 thread with 0 locks**.

## Architecture & Design

1. **Single-Threaded `io_uring`**:
   - Initialized with `IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER | IORING_SETUP_COOP_TASKRUN | IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN`.
   - Pre-registers the descriptor table via `IORING_REGISTER_FILES` (`IOSQE_FIXED_FILE`) with dynamic kernel-buffer leasing via `io_uring_setup_buf_ring` (`IOSQE_BUFFER_SELECT`).
   - Connection state (`conn_slot_t`) is packed to 16 bytes (1.04 MB for 65,536 slots) with an asynchronous partial-packet pool to reassemble split TCP segments without blocking.
2. **Durability & Group Commit (Rule 6)**:
   - Uses on-disk SQLite with `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;`, `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;`, and `PRAGMA locking_mode = EXCLUSIVE;`.
   - Requests arriving in the same `io_uring` completion batch are processed within a single `BEGIN IMMEDIATE; ... COMMIT;` transaction. Responses (`201 Created` / `200 OK`) queue for transmission only after `COMMIT` finishes.
   - Read cursors reset immediately after row extraction to avoid pinning WAL snapshots.
3. **Auth & Query Path**:
   - Precomputes inner and outer HMAC-SHA256 key midstates at boot, utilizing hardware SHA-NI instructions (`#ifdef __SHA__`) with portable software fallback.
   - `GET /feed` traverses `posts_created_at_id_idx` in index order (`LIMIT 20`) with covering-index counts on `likes_post_id_idx`, formatting output with inline integer-to-ASCII routines and in-place HTTP header prepending.
4. **Compilation**:
   - Compiles `server.c` and SQLite amalgamation together with `-O3 -flto -fno-plt -march=native`.
   - Runs a 50,000-cycle `--pgo-train` pass across all 5 endpoints to enable cross-unit branch inlining.

## Verification

- Passes **42/42** functional tests via `test/run.sh`.
- Stress-tested to **64,000 concurrent VUs** using k6 in a 1-vCPU, 2,048 MB RAM (0 swap) container (`--cpus=1.0 --memory=2048m`).

title: Add ruby-async-cicloid submission
body:
Adds `submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/`: Ruby 4.0.7 + YJIT on the [async](https://github.com/socketry/async) reactor (io-event, io_uring selector) with a small HTTP/1.1 layer of its own, **direct** on `0.0.0.0:80`.

## Highlights

- **Idle connections own no fiber.** Keep-alive connections sit in an edge-triggered epoll set (bound through FFI) and cost about 3–5 KB each. A pool of 256 worker fibers (growing only if every worker is busy) serves ready connections, so GC no longer scans tens of thousands of fibers. That GC cost is what held back the first, Falcon-based version.
- **io_uring for socket reads and writes**, through the fiber scheduler, so they are submitted in batches instead of one syscall each.
- **SQLite renders every response** with `json_object` / `group_concat`. Statements are prepared once and reset right after use. Leaving them mid-step held a read transaction open, which blocked WAL checkpoints and let the WAL grow past 300 MB under load.
- **`p.id=+?` in the single-post join.** With a plain `?`, SQLite recompiled that statement on every request; the `+` keeps the same plan and output and halves the query (14 → 7 µs).
- **Group commit.** Writes in one reactor pass share one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE … COMMIT`, and every response waits for its commit. WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`, `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, passive checkpoints on a 1 s timer off the commit path.
- **SQLite 3.54.0 built from the amalgamation with profile-guided optimization**, trained on the server's own statements in the load test's mix, and statically linked into extralite.
- **JWT HS256 verified on every request** with libsodium's HMAC-SHA256 (via rbnacl), 1.6 µs, constant-time compare. No caching across requests.
- Ruby, SQLite and libsodium are built from source at pinned versions with SHA-256 checks; every gem is pinned with checksums.

## Verification

- `test/run.sh`: **42/42 pass** on x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04, clean VM). `install.sh` takes about 10 min on one vCPU; `start.sh` is healthy in about a second.
- Extra HTTP edge cases checked: pipelining across a group commit, partial reads, HTTP/1.0, `Connection: close`.

## Load results

Proxmox VMs: target with 1 dedicated Zen 3 vCPU, 2 GB, no swap, nofile 65535; separate 8-vCPU load VM. That vCPU is faster than a droplet's, so these are relative numbers. All runs use the unmodified `bench/load.js` request mix.

**k6, target capped at half a core** (Proxmox `cpulimit=0.5`) as a rough droplet stand-in, 60 s ramp, 2 min hold:

| VUs | p95 | p99 | Failed | req/s | RSS | Thresholds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35,000 | 16 ms | 48 ms | 0% | 2,911 | 137 MB | pass |
| 40,000 | 216 ms | 526 ms | 0% | 3,315 | 159 MB | pass |
| 45,000 | 1.15 s | 1.96 s | 0% | 3,528 | 201 MB | fail |

**Uncapped, side by side with other entries** on the same VM (C connection generator from PR #14, 8 processes; CPU is the whole VM):

| Server | 25k users | 40k users |
|---|---|---|
| **This server** | 27% CPU, 117 MB, p95/p99 2 / 10 ms | 40%, 130 MB, 6 / 28 ms |
| Python + Granian (#41) | 47%, 428 MB, 5 / 26 ms | 70%, 661 MB, 169 / 1,660 ms |
| Go net/http (#18) | 59%, 536 MB, 7 / 23 ms | 93%, 578 MB, 194 / 1,718 ms |
| Python lean FastAPI (#10) | 58%, 289 MB, 10 / 149 ms | 88%, 421 MB, 370 / 2,887 ms |
| Python FastAPI (#1) | 80%, 367 MB, 82 / 1,436 ms | 99%, 12k failed requests |

None of this was measured on a droplet; the README has the details and caveats.

## Trade-offs

Linux only (epoll via FFI); no idle timeout; the parser covers what this API needs (no chunked request bodies, no `Expect: 100-continue`); reads use `IO::Buffer`, which Ruby still marks experimental.

Only `submissions/ruby-async-cicloid/` is added.

title: Java quarkus panama raisinsfried
body:
I wanted to try and hit the 64k wall with Java using a full heavy framework no custom JSON/Header parsing nonsense a full proper production setup with full synchronous, but I failed kind of, any speed above around 61.5k is unreliable. I also wanted to keep the program line count reasonable. 

I had 1 pass at 64k but 3 other runs i could only hit 61,500, I am fairly confident with some GC tweaks it can be done 

| | |
|---|---|
| Language | Java 27 (Eclipse Temurin 27+35) |
| Framework | Quarkus 3.40.1 (Quarkus REST + Jackson, Vert.x 4.5.34, Netty 4.1.138, native epoll) |
| SQLite driver | none: Ubuntu's SQLite 3.45.1 called through Java's Foreign Function & Memory API |
| JSON | Jackson 2.21.7 + Blackbird |
| JWT | auth0 java-jwt 4.6.1 |
| **Nginx or direct** | **Direct**: serves `0.0.0.0:80` itself |


## Optimizations, and why

- **[Panama](https://youtu.be/2wHU5ocfFsA?list=RD2wHU5ocfFsA)** Faster then JNI for SQLlite
- **One event loop.** Endpoints are `@NonBlocking`
- **`synchronous=FULL` Actually an unoptimization
- **Pragmas:** WAL, `synchronous=FULL`, 16 MiB page cache, `mmap_size=0`, `temp_store=MEMORY`.
- **JSON:** Jackson with Blackbird (~2% fewer instructions per request).
- **JVM:** G1 with a fixed 384 MB young generation (`-Xmx1g -Xmn384m`): ~40% fewer young pauses than G1's own sizing,
  which halved p99 at 61.5k users; `MaxDirectMemorySize=128m`.

## My testing and Results on a $12 droplet
1 vCPU / 2 GB (syd1)


| Users | p95 | p99 | Errors | Server CPU busy | Java RSS | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 61,500 | 199 ms | 400 ms | 0% | 80% | 560 MB | pass |
| 62,000 | 218 ms | 1.96 s | 0% | 83% | 558 MB | fail (p99) |
| 63,000 | 546 ms | 1.07 s | 0% | 81% | 566 MB | fail (p95, p99) |
| 64,000 | 334 ms | 574 ms | 0% | 84% | 568 MB | pass |



## Disclosures
My Java skills are mostly pretty rusty, I am a sysadmin I mostly manage other peoples Java apps, but it was the language I learned in school, did have to lean on an LLM a bit to fill in the gaps and speed up development.

title: Add csharp-epoll-gichamba (C#, Native AOT, epoll, SQLite, direct)
body:
C# compiled with Native AOT, serving HTTP itself on epoll. Direct, no Nginx. No NuGet packages. SQLite 3.53.4 is built from source and linked into the binary.

## How it works

- **One thread does everything.** The box has one core, so more threads only add context switches.
- **Group commit.** Each epoll wake-up is one batch in one SQLite transaction. The batch commits once, then the responses go out. Every 201 is sent after its row is committed (rule 6).
- **WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`.** Checkpoints run after the responses are sent, not inside COMMIT.
- **One reused buffer.** The status line, headers and JSON are written straight into it. The JWT is verified on every request (rule 5).

`test/run.sh` passes all 42 checks on Ubuntu 24.04.

## What I measured

These are not official scores. They come from an Azure Standard_F1s (1 vCPU, 2 GB, Ubuntu 24.04), with the unchanged `bench/load.js` run by k6 from a separate VM. Each result is a 5-minute hold.

| Entry | Users held | p99 | Server CPU |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| PR #27, C# on raw Kestrel | 56,000 | 615 ms | not recorded |
| This entry | 64,000 | 53 ms | 39% |

64,000 is the box's limit, not the server's: the kernel's connection-tracking table holds 65,536 entries, and the server still had most of the CPU free.

I also ran this entry against PR #60, a C# entry on io_uring, on a fresh box of the same size. Each ran twice at 64,000 users:

| Entry | p99 | Server CPU | Server memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| This entry | 51 to 53 ms | 41 to 42% | about 290 MB |
| PR #60 | 17 to 42 ms | 65 to 66% | about 1 GB |

PR #60 answers faster. This entry does the same work with about 40% less CPU and about a third of the memory. The score only needs p95 under 500 ms and p99 under 1 s, so on the slower droplet I'd expect the spare CPU to count for more than the lower latency.

## Credit

The request validation and the JWT verifier are adapted from maks-march's C# entry, PR #27.

body:
### Summary
This PR adds a pure **x86_64 Assembly (NASM)** web server using raw Linux `epoll` (`submissions/asm-epoll-FlavouredTux/`) for the $12 Server Challenge.

### Architecture & Design
- **Language & Runtime:** Pure x86_64 Assembly (NASM ELF64, Intel syntax)
- **I/O Multiplexing:** Raw Linux `epoll` (`epoll_create1`, `epoll_ctl`, `epoll_wait`) with non-blocking sockets (`SOCK_NONBLOCK | SOCK_CLOEXEC`)
- **Memory Management:** Zero dynamic heap allocation (`malloc`/`free`) in the request path; direct array lookup via demand-paged `mmap` connection table
- **Database Driver:** Direct C ABI binding to SQLite (`libsqlite3.so`) using pre-prepared statements (`sqlite3_prepare_v2`)
- **Crypto & Auth:** OpenSSL `libcrypto.so` (`HMAC`, `EVP_sha256()`) with hand-rolled Base64URL encoder/decoder executed in CPU registers
- **Deployment Mode:** **Direct (`0.0.0.0:80`)** — handles keep-alive connections natively and employs adaptive pressure-based socket eviction under high load, saving the 14–20% CPU overhead of Nginx on 1 vCPU (also supports running behind Nginx on `127.0.0.1:3000`).

### Compliance Checklist
- [x] Adds exactly one folder: `submissions/asm-epoll-FlavouredTux/`
- [x] Contains `install.sh`, `build.sh`, `start.sh`, `README.md`, and `.gitignore`
- [x] No modifications to files outside `submissions/`
- [x] Passes all 42 tests in `test/test.sh` (100% green via `test/run.sh`)
- [x] Strictly adheres to Rule 5 (zero cross-request caching, dynamic HMAC-SHA256 signature verification)
- [x] Strictly adheres to Rule 6 (WAL mode, `synchronous=NORMAL`, durable writes)

title: Add go-epoll-champ3oy submission (Go, io_uring direct descriptors, SQLite in C, direct)
body:
Adds `submissions/go-epoll-champ3oy/`: a Go server on a hand-written event loop, with io_uring for I/O and all the SQLite work done in C.

**Nginx or direct:** direct, on `0.0.0.0:80`.

### Past the 65,535 file-descriptor limit in one process
Client sockets are **io_uring direct descriptors**. They're accepted straight into a ring's registered file table and never get a file descriptor. The kernel limits each table to `RLIMIT_NOFILE` entries, but per table, not in total. So the server drives **two rings from one thread**: 2 × 65,535 connection slots in one process. With 100k connections open, it had 48 file descriptors.

If io_uring isn't available (sysctl, seccomp, old kernel), the same server falls back to epoll, which holds about 65k connections.

### The rest
- One event loop on one thread; idle connections hold no receive buffer (multishot recv into a shared provided-buffer pool); one `io_uring_enter` per loop iteration.
- SQLite 3.54.0 compiled in through cgo (`build.sh` downloads it and checks its SHA-256). Each request makes one Go→C call that runs the prepared statement and writes the JSON straight into the response buffer.
- **Group commit**: likes and new posts from one batch share a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE … COMMIT`, and their responses are sent only after it commits (rule 6). `synchronous=NORMAL`.
- WAL checkpoints run on a second thread. While one runs, writes wait (reads don't), so the WAL always rewinds and stays around 4 MB.
- JWT signatures are checked with `crypto/hmac` on every request (rule 5).

### Testing
- `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 on Ubuntu 24.04 with io_uring, with the automatic epoll fallback (Docker's default seccomp blocks io_uring), and with `SERVER_IO=epoll`. The epoll version also passed on x86_64.
- Local load tests (Docker on a Mac, server pinned to one core, 2 GB, `nofile=65535`): 60k users pass in 3 of 5 runs on each backend. A 100k run held all 100k connections but failed on latency (p99 38 s) while the load generators saturated the VM. I haven't been able to measure 65k+ fairly on real hardware yet; details are in the README.

| This one | 64,000 | pass | 78% | 271 / 427 ms |
| #27 (the C# entry in the community video), same setup | 34,000 | pass | 91% | 16 / 30 ms |

The README notes one operational detail: the server holds the database with `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, so stop it before opening the file with `sqlite3`.

title: rust io_uring version 2
body:
Version 2 of #19: direct Rust/io_uring HTTP with larger queues and receive buffers, earlier buffer returns, and bounded ENOBUFS retries. Successful write responses wait for SQLite commit; every request reads live data and every JWT signature is verified.

The JSON follow-up replaces production serde_json with a standalone LUFP-style cursor that validates complete documents, borrows ordinary strings, and checks escapes and Unicode. JWT headers and claims must be objects. Serde remains only as a development dependency for differential tests.

On Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL2 with one server CPU, 2 GiB/no swap and 65,535 descriptors, parsing is about twice as fast in repeated isolated tests. The longer six-pair comparison uses 1.3–3.7% less CPU per create request in every pair; feed and mixed changes remain within observed variation. This is a localized improvement, not an official capacity claim. Validation passes 42 official checks, six feed checks, ten Rust tests and 96 protocol/recovery checks including 15,000 sockets and 66-second reuse. The unchanged official k6 workload also passes a five-minute hold at 15,000 users with zero failed requests/checks. [Method, limitations and raw evidence](https://github.com/Scooter1337/twelve-dollar-server-challenge/blob/bdf985e/submissions/rust-epoll-scooter1337/LUFP.md).

The checkpoint follow-up raises the synchronous WAL checkpoint trigger from 1,000 to 4,096 frames. WAL/NORMAL and commit-before-response ordering remain unchanged. Six balanced pairs against LUFP alone, with one fixed SQLite archive, improve mixed throughput by 8.97% at 64 connections and 14.46% at 1,024; every mixed pair is positive. Normal production builds confirm +7.96% across six pairs at 64 connections, and +14.03%/+14.58% in two pairs at 1,024. CPU/request increases 1.3–5.9% at 64 and falls at 1,024; median p99 rises about 5–7 ms and peak cgroup memory increases about 14 MiB. The exact production source passes 42 official +6 feed +10 Rust +96 protocol/recovery checks and the unchanged 15,000-user five-minute hold: 559,968 requests/checks, zero failures, p95 0.407 ms, p99 2.01 ms. This remains an Ubuntu/WSL comparison, not an official droplet capacity result. [All candidate decisions, validation, production results and raw evidence](https://github.com/Scooter1337/twelve-dollar-server-challenge/blob/95aa405a0003599dbc7fb4dfa47a09e8343239df/submissions/rust-epoll-scooter1337/RESEARCH.md).

Grouped SQL counts, early send submission, thread/process checkpoint helpers, four single-issuer designs, a larger checkpoint interval, PASSIVE checkpoints and batching/wait changes were evaluated independently. Slower, inconsistent or correctness-failing versions are excluded from active server source; their sources and results are archived for review.

Earlier transport measurements on the native Xeon E5-2690 v3, one CPU/2 GiB: mixed median 47,660 versus C #55's 42,007 req/s (+13.5%). At 350k native users: +81.3% successful req/s and 41.3% lower peak memory. That historical comparison uses 1,048,576 descriptors and raises C's connection cap to match Rust; mixed median is 1.18% below the preceding Rust revision. These measurements predate the LUFP follow-up.

title: Add python-pypy-epoll-pranavds-codes submission
body:
Adds one folder, submissions/python-pypy-epoll-pranavds-codes/: Python on PyPy, no framework, serving port 80 directly.

## Stack
PyPy 7.3.15 (Ubuntu's pypy3 package) and the standard library only: a select.epoll HTTP/1.1 server, the stdlib sqlite3 module, and OpenSSL's HMAC() through PyPy's bundled cffi. No third-party packages, nothing downloaded at build time.

## Design
One epoll loop over raw sockets. Requests are parsed with bytes.find, and each response is one write().
SQLite builds the response JSON (json_object / group_concat, returned as bytes), so no Python serializer runs.
Keep-alive budget: above 25,000 open sockets, replies carry Connection: close and the server closes first. Users are then limited by CPU, not by LimitNOFILE=65535 or the client's ports.
Cheap reconnects: TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT and accept4. A connection being retired is answered and closed without entering epoll (4 syscalls).
No per-connection objects, so idle keep-alive connections cost almost nothing.
Every request runs its own SQL and verifies its JWT. Every write commits before its 201 (WAL, synchronous=NORMAL).

## Results
- My VM (4-vCPU Xeon, server pinned to one core, load over loopback), bench/load.js user loop with the official profile (60 s ramp, 5-minute hold): 160,000 users pass. p95 173 ms, p99 310 ms, 1 error in 5.06 M requests, 84% server CPU. At 170,000 users, p99 was 1,075 ms, just over the limit.
- Independent run: #41's author benchmarked this PR at its current commit (87b9283) on a Docker setup with the droplet's limits (1 CPU, 2 GB, 65,535 descriptors) and separate load-generator containers. 140,000 users pass with p99 17 ms, 61% CPU and 460 MiB, at 51 µs of server CPU per request. That is the lowest of the Python entries measured there (#41 73–81 µs, #10 81 µs, #13 120 µs, #1 130 µs). Details are in #41's README.


## Tests
test/run.sh: 42/42. Also 25 raw-socket HTTP edge cases (bench/http_edge.py), and #13's 78 extra checks plus 16 concurrent likes.
Design notes, full tables and how to reproduce them are in the README.

title: Add java-virtualthreads-Ahosan1Siam submission (Java 21+, raw sockets…
body:
I wanted to see how far we could push modern Java without relying on heavy enterprise frameworks or reactive complexity. I took inspiration from a telecom billing system architecture (CBS) I work on, using Java 21+ Virtual Threads on raw sockets with zero third-party framework dependencies, custom zero-allocation JSON streaming, and SQLite group commits to see if we can glide past the 64k connection ceiling.

| | |
|---|---|
| Language | Java 21 LTS (compatible up to Java 25+) |
| Framework | None. A custom raw HTTP/1.1 micro-engine on `ServerSocket` |
| Concurrency | Java Virtual Threads (`Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`) |
| SQLite driver | `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` 3.49.1.0 (bundled SQLite 3.49.1) |
| JSON | None. Custom zero-allocation parser + SQLite's native `json_object` |
| JWT | None. Custom pure Java HMAC-SHA256 validator (no external auth libraries) |
| **Nginx or direct** | **Direct**: serves `0.0.0.0:80` itself |

## Optimizations, and why

- **Virtual Threads for 66k+ connections:** Traditional platform threads take 1 MB stack each, which would burn 66 GB of RAM. Virtual threads unmount from the single carrier thread when blocked waiting on client think times (3–15 s). 66,000 idle connections consume less than 30 MB of heap memory.
- **Breaking past the 65,535 FD limit:** When open connections approach 60,000, `ConnectionTracker` evicts the longest-idle connection with `SO_LINGER=0` (sends a TCP RST to avoid `TIME_WAIT`). Because virtual users spend most of their time in think time, an evicted client simply reconnects transparently on its next click.
- **SQLite Group Commit:** Writes (`POST /posts` and `/like`) go into a single-writer queue that batches all pending requests in an event cycle into one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT`. All 201 responses wait for their commit (Rule 6 compliant), avoiding disk write stalls while keeping full durability.
- **8-Connection Reader Pool:** Read queries run on a dedicated pool with `PRAGMA query_only = ON` and prepared statements, serving `/feed` and `/posts/:id` in microseconds.
- **JSON built in SQL:** `/feed` queries use SQLite's native `json_object()` and index lookups (`posts_created_at_id_idx`), streaming formatted JSON straight to the socket buffer with zero Java object reflection or Jackson overhead.
- **Pragmas:** WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`, 64 MiB page cache, 1 GiB `mmap_size`, `temp_store=MEMORY`, `foreign_keys=ON`.
- **JVM:** Serial GC (`-XX:+UseSerialGC -Xms256m -Xmx512m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders`). On 1 vCPU, concurrent collectors waste CPU cycles on background threads.

## My testing and Results

Tested locally against all 42 checks in `test/test.sh`:
- Special characters / Unicode (`café ✓`) and whitespace trimming pass.
- Foreign key violation on missing post like correctly returns `404` without extra queries.
- Instant 1-second build via standard `javac` (single 14 MB self-contained jar, zero framework bloat).

| Test | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | Pass | 200 with DB uptime |
| `GET /feed` | Pass | 20 newest posts with exact key order |
| `GET /posts/:id` | Pass | 200 on found, 404 on missing, 400 on invalid id |
| `POST /posts` | Pass | 201 with trimmed body & valid token check |
| `POST /posts/:id/like` | Pass | 201 on first like, 200 on repeat, 404 on missing post |

## Disclosures
Code borrows architectural patterns from a high-throughput telecom central billing system (CBS) we maintain, stripped down to raw sockets and virtual threads specifically for this 1 vCPU / 2 GB challenge. Leaned on AI pair-programming to wire up the group commit batching and strict test suite golden matchers.

title: Add NASM x86-64 direct HTTP submission
body:
Adds a Linux x86-64 NASM server with direct HTTP, assembly JSON/JWT/HS256 processing, and checksum-pinned source-built SQLite 3.54.0. Raw io_uring has an epoll fallback; one SQLite owner drives up to eight registered-file rings. Frozen read/write batches commit before successful writes or dependent reads are released.

Startup enables and verifies WAL, synchronous=NORMAL and foreign_keys=ON. The submission uses the four specified environment variables, root installation, normal-user build and foreground startup. No application data/token cache, schema changes, CPU affinity or host kernel tuning.

### Validation

- Official checks: **42/42** on io_uring and epoll; healthy within 0.25 seconds.
- Crypto/JSON differential tests, guard pages, canaries and ABI checks.
- SQL ordering/membership fixtures; mixed valid/invalid writes, duplicate likes, failed COMMIT/transaction rollback and acknowledged-write SIGKILL recovery.
- Aggregate memory-pressure recovery and multi-ring live-socket validation.

### Local five-minute confirmation

Unchanged bench/load.js, 1,000-user two-minute warmup, 60-second ramp and five-minute hold:

| Users | Requests | HTTP/check failures | p95 | p99 | Peak server memory |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **275,000** | 10,264,833 | **0 / 0** | 16.233 ms | 65.394 ms | 1,446 MiB |

Ubuntu 24.04 container userspace on a Threadripper 7960X / Linux 7.0.0-38-generic host; server limited to one CPU, 2 GiB, no swap and nofile=65,535. k6 1.4.2 ran in a separate container on the same physical host, using private loopback. The host OS is outside the server quota; Docker required a disclosed seccomp exception for io_uring.

This is a selected-count local confirmation, **not an organizer score, maximum-user search or proven win over the eligible field**. Recent short screens varied: the default-generator NASM/#75 pair failed latency, while a matched generator-parallelism-12 NASM/Rust-#82 pair passed at 275k (p99 429.6/559.0 ms). Short screens and five-minute confirmations are kept distinct. Full results, exact artifact/source hashes and remaining qualification limits are in PERFORMANCE.md and research/qualification-evidence.json.

Unadopted scheduling/serialization prototypes remain local experiments; this PR submits the measured baseline.

title: Add java-nio-stohirov submission
body:
Adds `submissions/java-nio-stohirov/`: Java 25 with no framework. A single-threaded HTTP/1.1 server runs on Linux `epoll`, and both sockets and SQLite 3.54.0 are called through FFM, with no `java.nio` and no JDBC. It serves port 80 directly, with no Nginx, and has zero Java dependencies. This replaces #58; design notes are in the submission README.

**Tests:** `test/run.sh` passes 42/42 on `0600708` in a clean Ubuntu 24.04 container. The server was also checked on x86_64 and arm64 (`struct epoll_event` is laid out differently on each): pipelining, split requests, `Connection: close`, HTTP/1.0 and eviction.

## Stats

Measured locally, not on the droplet: Docker on Apple Silicon, with the server pinned to 1 CPU, 2 GiB RAM, no swap and `nofile=65535`.

### Max users (README protocol: one keep-alive connection per user, `load.js` think times, 60 s ramp, 2 min hold)

| Users | Result | req/s | Server CPU | p95 | p99 | Errors |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 128,000 | pass | 13,543 | 31% | 11 ms | 28 ms | 0.011% |
| 256,000 | pass | 27,086 | 56% | 38 ms | 55 ms | 0.0013% |
| 320,000 | pass | 33,808 | 69% | 57 ms | 68 ms | 0.0009% |
| 352,000 | pass | 37,106 | 76% | 90 ms | 127 ms | 0.0006% |
| **384,000** | **pass** | **40,578** | 78% | 119 ms | 176 ms | 0.0075% |
| 416,000 | fail | ~40k | 82% | 369 ms | 6.7 s | 0.34% |

### Effect of each change

| Version | CPU at 256k users | p99 at 320k users | Highest level passed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Original + feed query restructure | 69% | 524 ms | 320k |
| + `SO_LINGER=0` on evicted connections | 64% | 160 ms | 320k |
| + sockets/epoll through FFM | **56%** | **68 ms** | **384k** |

### Closed-loop throughput (`load.js` mix, no think time, 64 connections, 3 rounds)

| Version / runtime | req/s | p99 | CPU-s per 10k req | RSS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Original, Temurin 25 JIT | 52.0k | 3.54 ms | 0.123 | 391 MB |
| Current, Temurin 25 JIT | **58.9k** | 3.40 ms | **0.104** | 396 MB |
| Current, Temurin 27 JIT | 57.4k | 3.56 ms | 0.104 | 399 MB |
| Current, GraalVM 25 native image + PGO | ~14.0k | ~9.5 ms | 0.655 | 29 MB |

Most of the RSS is the pre-touched 256 MB heap. Native image loses because FFM downcall handles can't be inlined ahead of time.

### With `LimitNOFILE` raised to 1M (no eviction)

| Users | Server CPU | p99 | Longest GC pause | Live heap | Peak memory |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 256,000 | 40% | 35 ms | 9 ms | 10 MB | 1.36 GiB |
| 384,000 | 64% | 262 ms | 12 ms | 18 MB | 1.89 GiB |

The heap holds about 40 bytes per connection. Kernel socket memory, at about 3.5 KB per connection, is the real ceiling: roughly 400k users in 2 GiB.

**Latest commit (`0600708`):** eviction now starts 128 descriptors below `LimitNOFILE` (65,407 connections), not 1,024 below it. That keeps it above the droplet's 65,536-entry conntrack ceiling. The benchmarks above ran on `3cc06f6`. This commit only moves the eviction threshold.

title: Add bash-socat-framegrace submission (pure Bash + socat + SQLite coprocess)
body:
### Bash + socat + SQLite Coprocess Submission

A minimalist, extreme-performance submission written in pure GNU Bash using `socat` for connection multiplexing and persistent `sqlite3` interactive coprocesses.

- **Language / Runtime:** GNU Bash 5.2+ (Ubuntu 24.04 stock)
- **Framework:** None (pure built-in Bash parameter expansion & built-ins)
- **Database Driver:** `sqlite3` CLI (v3.45+) via bidirectional coprocess file descriptors (`coproc SQLITE`)
- **Network Multiplexer:** `socat` (v1.8+) with Linux memory pipes (`EXEC:...,pipes` & 64KB buffers)
- **Mode:** Behind Nginx (`bench/nginx.conf` on `127.0.0.1:3000`)
- **Correctness:** Passes 100% of tests in `test/test.sh` (42/42 tests passing with byte-fidelity golden reads)
- **Peak Benchmark Score:** **25,500 VUs** (1,913.9 req/s, p95 = 58.9 ms, p99 = 643.9 ms, 0.00% error rate)

#### Key Architectural Highlights
1. **Zero-Subshell Hot Path:** Replaced command substitutions with dedicated output variables (`SQL_OUT`, `AUTH_OUT`, `AUTH_UID`, `AUTH_USER`, `B64_OUT`), eliminating thousands of `clone()` subshells per second.
2. **Persistent SQLite Coprocess (`coproc SQLITE`):** Single long-lived `sqlite3 -batch` instance per worker with 256 MB shared memory map (`PRAGMA mmap_size`), WAL mode, and busy timeout handling.
3. **Pure Glob Routing:** Replaced POSIX regex with native Bash glob pattern matching.
4. **Single Round-Trip Writes:** Multi-statement atomic SQL for post creation and likes, cutting SQLite coprocess IPC round-trips by 50%.
5. **In-SQLite Base64 Decoding & Claims Validation:** Zero-fork token decoding and claims verification using SQLite 3.45+ native `base64()` and `json_extract()`.
6. **Linux Direct Memory Pipe Buffering:** Replaced default BSD `socketpair` in `socat` with unidirectional Linux `pipes` (`EXEC:...,pipes`) and 64KB circular page-cache buffers.

## Submission: bash-builtin-framegrace

A high-performance pure-Bash server that achieves **100% zero-fork execution across all request paths** by combining `socat` Linux memory pipes, a persistent bidirectional `sqlite3` interactive coprocess, and a dynamic C loadable builtin (`enable -f hmac_b64.so hmac_b64`) calling OpenSSL `libcrypto` directly in the Bash process memory space.

### Architecture Highlights

1. **Zero-Fork JWT Cryptographic Verification:**
   - In stock Bash scripts, cryptographic HMAC-SHA256 signature verification requires spawning external subshells or sub-processes (`openssl dgst`), costing ~1.5ms per request and saturating the single vCPU at high concurrency.
   - Using GNU Bash's built-in dynamic module mechanism (`enable -f`), `hmac_b64.c` exposes an in-process builtin that directly hashes and base64url-encodes the token in **6.9 µs** (over 200x faster than process invocation).
2. **Persistent Interactive SQLite Coprocess (`coproc SQLITE`):**
   - Each keep-alive worker maintains a single long-lived `sqlite3 -batch` instance with synchronous WAL mode, in-memory temp store, and connection-level statement isolation compatible with SQLite 3.45.1.
   - Claims parsing and base64 decoding happen entirely in SQLite's native C implementation via `base64()` and `json_extract()`.
3. **Pure Glob HTTP Router & Parameter Expansions:**
   - Zero subshell forks across request parsing, HTTP method matching, and route handling.
4. **Linux Direct Memory Pipe Multiplexing:**

body:
Adds `submissions/python-cython-adeland/`, a Python/Cython implementation of the five challenge endpoints that serves HTTP/1.1 directly without Nginx or an ASGI framework. Python configures startup; one native reactor handles parsing, dispatch, SQLite, and response transmission outside the GIL.

- Bounds application request/output storage with a 128 MiB arena, aligned connection records, lazy request buffers, and chunked scatter/gather output that retains ownership across partial sends.
- Executes fresh SQL and verifies every protected request's HS256 signature. Prepared statements and keyed HMAC setup are reused; writes complete before success responses using SQLite WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`.

- Pressure tests: 15,000 idle connections held without drops; recovery after arena pressure from 8,000 incomplete bodies, with no OOM event.

- **Auth & JSON:** Zero-allocation HS256 HMAC verification with pre-computed inner/outer SHA-256 state pads (~80ns per verify). Zero-copy JSON parsing and streaming serialization into registered buffer pools.

- Official test runner (`test/run.sh`): **42/42 checks passed (100%)** on Ubuntu 24.04.

title: Add go-nethttp-mattn-vedic submission (Go, epoll, direct SQLite JSON)
body:
Adds and iterates on `submissions/go-nethttp-mattn-vedic/`, a Linux Go server tuned for the challenge's constrained single-vCPU environment.

## What makes this attempt special

- A Linux epoll loop handles HTTP/1.1 keep-alive sockets, while a bounded worker pool handles requests and SQLite calls. One request per connection is in flight at a time, preserving response order.
- The event loop avoids redundant epoll interest updates, reuses small per-connection read buffers, and drops oversized buffers after requests. `sendmsg` writes response headers and JSON bodies from separate buffers to avoid a response-sized copy.
- SQLite uses a local `go-sqlite3` fork and direct connection/statement APIs, without `database/sql`. `SQLiteStmt.QueryText` resets and binds a prepared statement, steps it, and copies the JSON result into a reusable Go buffer in one cgo call. SQLite's amalgamation is not vendored; the build links Ubuntu's system SQLite.
- Every request reads current values from SQLite; there is no application response or table-data cache. Authenticated requests verify HS256 JWTs every time, using pooled scratch space for decoding and HMAC state.
- One HTTP worker is the default for the 1-CPU target. Worker and database pool sizes remain configurable. The server listens directly, without requiring Nginx.

## Validation and profiling

- `bash test/run.sh submissions/go-nethttp-mattn-vedic`: 42/42 checks passed against the system SQLite library.
- A profiled 20,000-VU run used a server cgroup limited to 1 CPU and 2 GiB, four loopback aliases, a 30-second ramp, 2-minute hold, and 30-second ramp-down. It completed with zero failed requests at 1,760 requests/s, p95 0.269 ms, and p99 0.633 ms. Server cgroup memory peaked at about 166 MiB. This was a profiling run, not a maximum-capacity score.
- An 80,000-VU diagnostic run reached the target with all checks passing during the observed interval: about 7,080 requests/s, p95 6.56 ms, and p99 45.94 ms. The local k6 process grew to about 22.4 GiB RSS, so a host-memory guard stopped it after about 63 seconds. It did not complete the required five-minute hold and is not presented as an 80k pass.
- The 80k CPU profile sampled 11.08 CPU-seconds over 30 seconds: 50.8% flat in `runtime.cgocall` and 34.8% in `Syscall6`. These profiles guide further work but describe only the short observed interval.

Detailed setup, limitations, and profiles are recorded in the submission README and local benchmark artifacts.

title: Add java-raw-agrison submission (Java 27, virtual threads, FFM + SQLite)
body:
## submissions/java-raw-agrison

Java 27 with no framework and no dependencies — the JDK, plus SQLite compiled from source on the box.

| | |
|---|---|
| Language / runtime | Java 27 — OpenJDK 27 GA (`27+35`), pinned by SHA-256 |
| Framework | none (`ServerSocketChannel`, virtual threads, `java.lang.foreign`) |
| Database / driver | SQLite 3.54.0, built from the pinned amalgamation, bound with **FFM (Panama)**. No JDBC |
| JSON | **SQLite** writes every value (`json_object`); a hand-written strict RFC 8259 scanner reads the JWT payload |
| **Nginx or direct** | **Direct** on `0.0.0.0:80`. Runs behind Nginx unchanged — it only reads `HOST`/`PORT` |

**`test/run.sh` → 42/42** on a fresh seed database.

### Approach

One virtual thread per connection, blocking I/O. Requests are parsed in place in a direct `ByteBuffer` — no `String` on any hot path. Every value that comes from the database is serialised by SQLite's `json_object` and copied straight from SQLite's own buffer into the response buffer with `MemorySegment.copy`, so the server only writes the fixed frames around it. 
The response header is written *backwards* into reserved headroom, making each reply a single `write()` with an exact
`Content-Length`. Writes go to one dedicated platform thread that group-commits, and every request waits for its own commit (WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`), so a 201 always means the row is on disk.

Measured 43 bytes allocated per request — identical for `/nope` (no SQL at all) and `/feed` (20 rows + 20 native copies), i.e. the handlers allocate nothing; the residue is the JDK's NIO read path.
200k GETs produced zero young GCs.

### Verification

Built and run from a bare `ubuntu:24.04` container with nothing preinstalled: `install.sh` → JDK 27+35 (checksum verified), `build.sh` → `libsqlite3.so` + `javac --release 27` (checksum verified), `start.sh` → healthy in **281 ms**, `test/test.sh` → **42/42**.

On a `--cpus=1 --memory=2g` container with k6 in a sibling container — a proxy, *not* the droplet — a 5-minute hold at **20,000 VUs**: 1,868 req/s, p95 1.09 ms, p99 2.39 ms, **0.00% errors**, 785 MB RSS, mean 23.7% of the single vCPU. I could not push past 20k locally: k6 itself runs out of ephemeral ports first.

I wanted to see how raw Java we could go, and curious to see the final numbers when you run it for real !

title: Add node-uwebsockets-zahidcakici submission (Node.js 24, uWebSockets.js, better-sqlite3; direct on :80)
body:
## Submission: `submissions/node-uwebsockets-zahidcakici`

| | |
|---|---|
| Runtime | Node.js v24.21.0 LTS (official tarball, SHA-256 verified, in `/opt/node-v24.21.0`) |
| HTTP server | uWebSockets.js v20.71.0, **compiled from source** at pinned commits (uWebSockets.js `127ac80`, uWebSockets `1d80f7a`, uSockets `86097c4`) |
| SQLite driver | better-sqlite3 13.0.3, **compiled from source** (bundled SQLite 3.53.4; npm prebuilds deleted) |
| Nginx or direct | **Direct** on `0.0.0.0:80`, one process, one thread |

### Key optimizations
- **uWebSockets.js instead of `node:http`**: HTTP is parsed in C++, with one JS call per request and no per-request streams or objects.
- **Keep-alive fix**: uWebSockets hard-codes a 10 s HTTP timeout. k6 users think for 8–23 s, so they kept reconnecting, and some POSTs failed. `build.sh` patches `HTTP_IDLE_TIMEOUT_S` and `HTTP_TIMEOUT_S` to 75 s. At 20k users: 0 failed requests (was 307) and p99 28 ms (was 3.67 s).
- **SQLite builds the response JSON** (`json_object` + `group_concat`, `INSERT … RETURNING` for creates). One string goes straight to `res.end()`. There is no `ORDER BY` inside the aggregate, because the index already gives the order.
- **Group commit**: writes queued during one event-loop turn are committed in a single `BEGIN … COMMIT`. Responses are sent only after `COMMIT` returns.
- **SQLite tuning**: WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`, `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` (WAL index in heap, no fcntl locks; +5%), `wal_autocheckpoint=4000` (4× fewer checkpoint fsyncs; +8% on write-heavy load), and mmap.
- **JWT HS256 checked on every request** with a `KeyObject` from `createSecretKey`, so the key isn't re-imported per call (+5%).
- **`--max-semi-space-size=64`**, and a connection budget read from `/proc/self/limits` so that `EMFILE` never makes the accept loop spin.

### Results
- `test/test.sh`: **42/42 passing** on x86_64 (CI-equivalent clean Ubuntu 24.04 run) and on arm64.
- Head-to-head against #78 (`node:net` + `node:sqlite`): k6 with 20k users and the server CPU capped to the same budget. For the same 207k requests this submission used **~18% less CPU** (14% vs 17%) and **~43% less memory** (112 MB vs 198 MB RSS). Tail latency was about half: p99 180–226 ms vs 392–417 ms. Neither had errors.

### Rules
No response, row or JWT caches (rule 5). A 201 means the row is committed (rule 6). Only in-process settings are tuned (rule 11). Details and all measurements are in the submission's README.

body:
Adds `submissions/fsharp-oxpecker-delneg/`: F# and Oxpecker on ASP.NET Core 10 / Kestrel, with SQLite 3.53.4 built from source.

- **Deployment**: direct on `HOST:PORT` (`0.0.0.0:80`), no Nginx.
- **Oxpecker**: `build.sh` builds it from [delneg/Oxpecker](https://github.com/delneg/Oxpecker) at commit `ef46b35` (branch `autoresearch/perf-2026-10-14`), without commit `c911ea1`.
- **`test/run.sh`**: 42/42 in a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container with 1 CPU, 2 GB and no swap, after `install.sh`. `install.sh` took 87 s. `test/run.sh` (build and tests) took 50 s.
- **Design**: one request thread and one SQLite connection for reads and autocommit writes. A second connection on a background thread runs the WAL checkpoints, so a slow fsync does not stop requests.

### Local hold

These numbers are local diagnostics, not an official score.

- Machine: a VM with 4 vCPUs of an Intel Core i5-11400F and 3.9 GB of RAM. Its disk has slow fsync (about 67 ms).
- Server: a Docker container with 1 CPU, 2 GB, no swap and `nofile` 65535.
- Load: kload (PR #87), a replay of `bench/load.js`, on the other 3 CPUs over loopback. 60 s warm-up at 1,000 users, 60 s ramp, then the hold.

| Users | Hold | Result | p95 / p99 | Errors | Server CPU | Requests/s | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 2 min | pass | 0.7 / 1.1 ms | 0 | 12% | 1,058 | 180 MB |
| 30,000 | 2 min | pass | 0.3 / 12 ms | 0 | 16% | 3,175 | 490 MB |
| 50,000 | 2 min | pass | 0.3 / 49 ms | 0 | 23% | 5,292 | 823 MB |
| 64,000 | 5 min | pass | 0.3 / 56 ms | 0 of 2.03M | 28% | 6,774 | 1,170 MB |

Second check on different hardware (64,000 users, 5-minute hold, same 1 CPU / 2 GB container):

| Machine | Commit | p99 (hold) | Errors | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| VM, Intel i5-11400F, fsync about 67 ms | `ce63f0e` | 56 ms | 0 of 2.03M | 1,170 MB |
| WSL2, AMD Ryzen 9 7900X3D, fsync about 2 ms | `60f3d3f` | 23 ms | 0 of 2.03M | 785 MB |

### Experiments

Each experiment had one change. The CPU column is server CPU for each request at a fixed request rate, as a ratio to the previous build.

| # | Change | Result | Kept |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | No zero-byte read in Kestrel | CPU -5% | yes |
| 2 | `route "/posts/{id}"` instead of `routef` | CPU -5% | yes |
| 3 | Native AOT | same CPU, 55 MB less RSS | no |
| 4 | Writer thread with group commit | p95 590 to 0.45 ms on the slow disk, but CPU +38% | no |
| 5 | Checkpoint thread with its own connection | p95 500 to 0.21 ms on the slow disk, CPU same | yes |
| 6 | Inlined `Monitor` lock | no change | no |
| 7 | Write semaphore for the WAL catch-up, so reads go on | 59.9k of 60k requests served instead of 58.0k | yes |
| 8 | SQLite at `-O3` | no change | no |
| 9 | `/feed` JSON built by SQLite | CPU +17% | no |
| 10 | 64 MB GC gen0 budget | no change | no |
| 11 | WAL catch-up at 256 MB instead of 64 MB | p95 272 to 1.7 ms at 62,000 users | yes |

Experiments 1 to 3 ran on an arm64 VM. The others ran on the x86-64 VM above.

title: Add Nim submission: direct HTTP/1.1 on SQLite (io_uring default, epoll fallback)
body:
Adds `submissions/nim-io_uring-NioHast/`.

## What it is
A single-threaded, direct HTTP/1.1 server in Nim 2.2.12 (compiled to C) with in-process SQLite 3.54.0.

- **Toolchain:** Nim 2.2.12, pinned binary toolchain installed by `install.sh` (sha256-verified).
- **Networking:** served directly on `HOST:PORT` via **io_uring by default**, with an always-built
  **edge-triggered epoll fallback**. Both transports share one HTTP layer (`src/http.nim`) and emit
  byte-identical responses.
- **Database:** SQLite 3.54.0 amalgamation, pinned download (sha256) compiled in-tree by `build.sh`, so
  there is no system `libsqlite3` dependency.
- **Auth:** HS256 JWT via HMAC-SHA256 (vendored nimcrypto 0.7.3, pure Nim).

## Transports
| Transport | How to select | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| **io_uring** (default) | nothing, or `TRANSPORT=io_uring` | completion-queue loop, provided-buffer receive pool, registered file descriptors |
| **epoll** (always available) | `TRANSPORT=epoll`, or automatic fallback | edge-triggered epoll; idle keep-alive eviction + RST close |

`start.sh` runs `bin/server_iouring` by default; if it is missing or exits before serving it falls back to
`bin/server`. The io_uring binary additionally re-execs `bin/server` itself when `io_uring_setup` fails at
run time, so a host that blocks io_uring never leaves the service down.

## Why this design
- **Why two transports:** io_uring wins on CPU and latency, but it can be unavailable at run time even on
  an identical OS image (container `seccomp` blocks the `io_uring_*` syscalls, a host `kernel.io_uring_disabled`
  sysctl, an LSM, or an older kernel). epoll is always present and battle-tested; keeping it as an automatic
  fallback means the service always starts and serves.
- **Why io_uring is the default:** it measured **~0.65x epoll's CPU at 10k users** (and ~0.55x at 20k) with
  better p50/p95/p99. Defaulting is safe because of a dual fallback: build time (a failed io_uring build ships
  the epoll-only binary, exit 0) and run time (a failed `io_uring_setup` re-execs the epoll binary). Per-feature
  failures short of that (a rejected setup flag, no multishot recv, no multishot/direct accept, no buf ring)
  degrade in place without a restart.

## Optimizations
- **Direct, no Nginx or framework:** the box is one vCPU and a reverse proxy or web framework costs a slice
  of it.
- **One event loop, one thread:** no worker pool, no per-request objects; one `send` per response with
  backpressure, and (epoll) drain-to-`EAGAIN`.
- **io_uring:** multishot accept (direct fixed-slot install) + multishot recv with a kernel
  provided-buffer ring + registered file descriptors, plus `SINGLE_ISSUER | DEFER_TASKRUN | COOP_TASKRUN`
  ring flags and batched completions.
- **SQLite:** one connection, statements prepared once (`SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT`); **JSON serialized in
  Nim** (not `json_object`); mmap + a small page cache; bounded WAL; **write group commit** (one transaction
  per event-loop pass, committed before the response).
- **Capacity:** idle keep-alive **eviction + RST**, a 4096 listen backlog, **`TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT`**, EMFILE
  backoff.
- **Build:** two-pass **PGO** (synthetic training, plain-build fallback), `-O3 -march=native
  -fno-semantic-interposition -fno-plt --stacktrace:off -d:lto`, and SQLite trims (`THREADSAFE=0`, `DQS=0`,
  `USE_ALLOCA=1`, `LIKE_DOESNT_MATCH_BLOBS`, `OMIT_DECLTYPE`, `OMIT_AUTOINIT`, `OMIT_*`, JSON1).
- **O(n) request parsing** (cursor-compacted, no per-request buffer shift).

## Correctness & robustness
- The handler is wrapped so no request can crash the process (any exception, including `Defect`s, becomes
  `500`); request ids are range-checked before arithmetic.
- Strict framing (Content-Length digits only, `Transfer-Encoding` rejected), bounded buffered I/O, and
  idle/stalled timeouts. Writes are committed before their response is sent.

## Validation
- Official suite: **42/42** on the default (io_uring) transport, on `TRANSPORT=epoll`, and the CI runs green.
- Unit tests: `test_db` (vs the seed DB and the `sqlite3` CLI), `test_jwt` (vs `openssl` vectors),
  `test_iouring` (io_uring ABI + SQE/CQE).
- Durability: a `201` survives `kill -9` and restart on the same database.
- Adversarial checks: fragmented/pipelined requests, slow readers, stalled half-open sockets, random
  malformed input, and connection churn (stable RSS/fd).
- Local A/B (indicative): io_uring uses ~0.65x epoll's CPU with better tails; the server holds 300k idle
  keep-alive connections on a dev box.

## Compliance with the rules
- SQLite only, in-process (2); no in-memory store, no external cache.
- No caching across requests (5).
- Durable before responding; no `synchronous=OFF` (6).
- No hard-coded responses / no benchmark detection (7).
- Direct bind, Nginx optional (9).
- Built from source with pinned deps; nothing prebuilt shipped (10).
- No kernel tuning, no pinning (11); only in-process settings (socket options, pragmas, compiler flags).

## Dependencies
Runtime: glibc only. Build: pinned downloads (Nim 2.2.12, SQLite 3.54.0, nimcrypto 0.7.3, all
sha256-verified) plus standard Ubuntu tools; no Nimble packages. See `docs/DEPENDENCIES.md`.

## Docs
`README.md` (including the "Why this design" and "Toggles" sections) and
`docs/{ARCHITECTURE,DEVELOPMENT,PERFORMANCE,DEPENDENCIES}.md`.

## Honest limitations
Local measurements are environment-limited (generator and server on one box, loopback) and are not the
organiser's numbers.

## Files added
`submissions/nim-io_uring-NioHast/` (source only; build output and vendored downloads are gitignored).

MIT, under the repository license.

body:
## What

A C submission: single-threaded-per-worker `io_uring` server (multishot accept/recv, provided buffer ring, direct-descriptor file tables of up to 65,535 slots each), SQLite inline with group commit, hand-written HTTP/JSON/HMAC-SHA256, PGO build for both SQLite and the server. Serves `0.0.0.0:80` directly, no Nginx. An `epoll` fallback (same request path) covers kernels without multishot io_uring or where io_uring is disabled.

## Notes

- One mutex serializes the database across workers, so on one vCPU they never compete.
- Group commit: responses produced while a batch transaction is open (reads included) wait for the commit; a failed commit replaces them with a 500.
- The feed uses three range scans when the newest 20 ids are close together, the reference query otherwise; every response comes from queries for that request.
- Memory guardrails: below ~192 MB usable, stop accepting; below ~96 MB, shed idle keep-alives.
- `build.sh` downloads liburing 2.15 and SQLite 3.54.0 pinned by SHA-256, trains PGO on a synthetic database and a synthetic request mix (no seed data), and falls back to a plain `-O3` build if any PGO step fails. A final smoke test requires a healthy `/health`.

## Numbers seen while building it

GitHub `ubuntu-24.04` runner (kernel 6.x, io_uring mode), server pinned to one core, k6 on the other three, fresh seed copy:

| Users | p95 | p99 | Failed | Requests |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10,000 | 4.3 ms | 7.1 ms | 0.00% | 111,575 |
| 20,000 | 6.2 ms | 8.6 ms | 0.00% | 223,249 |

(30,000 users on one runner is where k6 exhausts the loopback ephemeral ports, so that ceiling is the load generator, not the server.)

`test/test.sh` passes 42/42 locally and in CI. Thanks for a great challenge — the video breakdown of what each submission traded away was a great read.

title: Add v-epoll-i098 submission (V, raw epoll, SQLite; direct on :80)
body:
Adds `submissions/v-epoll-i098/`: the five endpoints in V 0.5.2 on a single-threaded raw `epoll` loop with the SQLite C API called directly. Direct mode (no Nginx).

## How it works

- One event loop and one SQLite connection for every request (`SQLITE_THREADSAFE=2`), WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`.
- Group commit per `epoll_wait` batch: every request in a batch runs in one transaction, and responses are written only after `COMMIT` succeeds. A failed commit closes the batch's connections instead of answering them.
- WAL checkpoints never run on the event loop. SQLite's auto-checkpoint runs inside `COMMIT` and does two `fsync`s, which stalls every connection on a single loop. Here a `sqlite3_wal_hook` only records the WAL size; at 1,000 frames (SQLite's default) a checkpointer thread with its own connection runs a PASSIVE checkpoint and reports back through an `eventfd` in the same epoll set. If frames were appended meanwhile, write requests are held for at most 20 ms (reads go on) so one small follow-up checkpoint can let the WAL restart. No data is kept in the process: only the checkpoint timing moves.
- Feed: the newest 20 ids from the `(created_at, id)` index, then one range scan for the rows and authors and one range scan on `likes_post_id_idx` for the counts; the reference query runs when the ids are spread out. All values are read from SQLite during the request.
- Every bearer token is verified on every request: HS256 only (OpenSSL HMAC-SHA256), constant-time signature compare, then `exp`, `sub` and `username`.
- Past 65,535 descriptors, the longest-idle connection with no work in flight is closed and the new one is accepted; the client reconnects on its next request.
- Prepared statements for every query and for `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`; JSON written by hand into reused buffers, keys in spec order; `EPOLLOUT` registered only while output is pending.

## Build

`install.sh` builds the V compiler from source at the pinned commit (`7647ce1`, tag 0.5.2) with its pinned C bootstrap (vlang/vc `7eb8c54`), and installs `libssl-dev`. `build.sh` downloads the SQLite 3.54.0 amalgamation, checks its SHA-256, compiles it and builds `bin/server`. `start.sh` runs the server in the foreground. It is healthy right after start.

## Validation

- `bash test/run.sh submissions/v-epoll-i098`: **42 passed, 0 failed**. `install.sh` and `build.sh` were run in a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container.
- Durability check: 20,000 `POST /posts` over 64 connections, all 201, `PRAGMA integrity_check` ok and the exact row count afterwards; the WAL stays small (11 MB) under a sustained write flood.
- Descriptor check: with the server limited to 256 descriptors, 600 keep-alive clients were all served, and the process used no CPU while idle.

## Load test

Unchanged `bench/load.js` (k6 v2.3.0), README protocol: 1,000-user warm-up, search from 2,500 doubling to a failure, bisect to 250 users (1-min holds), then a 5-min confirm hold. Server in a Docker `ubuntu:24.04` container with `--cpus=1 --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g --ulimit nofile=65535:65535`, direct mode, fresh seed copy; k6 on 8 other cores of the same shared x86_64 host (load average 30-100 from other jobs), one benchmark at a time.

| Build | Users (5-min hold) | p95 | p99 | Errors | Server CPU (peak / run avg) | Peak RSS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **this PR** (checkpoints on a second thread) | **81,250** | 498 ms | 695 ms | 0.00% | 99% / 49% | 125 MiB |
| same code with SQLite's inline auto-checkpoint | 61,750 | 222 ms | 612 ms | 0.00% | 99% / 37% | 174 MiB |

The run average includes the 60 s ramp and the 30 s ramp-down. The first failing 1-min search was 83,000; the 5-min holds from 82,750 down to 81,500 failed on p95 alone (523-544 ms, 0 errors). On the earlier build, `bpftrace` showed the loop blocked 8 ms to 4 s per checkpoint `fsync` with the CPU half idle; the final build is CPU-bound. The numbers are a local comparison on a shared machine, not the droplet score.

## Kept on purpose

- `install.sh` builds V from source instead of downloading the `v_linux.zip` release: the compiler version is pinned to a commit and built on the box like everything else.

I am new to open source, and this pull request was made with AI assistance.
