title: New Rust/Axum submission
body:
Rust, Axum, Hyper and SQLite, with one HTTP event loop and a dedicated SQL thread. Ten listening ports share the same database and application state. Multiple destination ports let one load-generator IP open more connections than a single destination port permits.

### Results

The load generator ran separately. Each run used a 60-second ramp, 60-second nominal user hold, then drain and grace. Reproducing these connection counts needs [mjc/twelve-dollar-benchmark](https://github.com/mjc/twelve-dollar-benchmark), or many parallel k6 instances with enough combined CPU and memory to keep up.

| Server setup | Users | Hold requests/s | Requests | Errors | p95 / p99 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Host under systemd limits | 500,000 | 52,678 | 5,964,750 | 0 | 51.42 / 462.23 ms |
| Ubuntu VM | 240,000 | 25,333 | 2,849,999 | 0 | 478.15 / 618.25 ms |

I set up the systemd service to compare service resource limits with a VM. It had a 2 GiB memory limit and a configured one-core quota, but measured hold CPU was 119.97% of one core. The host OS was outside that memory budget. The VM had one vCPU and 2 GiB for the whole guest. Different server revisions and recording also prevent treating the gap as a measurement of VM overhead alone.

The 500k repeat peaked at 108.67 MiB app RSS. The VM used 85.54% whole-VM CPU and peaked at 1,274.10 MiB whole-VM memory, measured as `MemTotal - MemAvailable`, including the OS and observer. Most of that memory was in the kernel, tracking open sockets and connections: unreclaimable kernel object storage alone occupied 770.06 MiB at the peak sample, versus 128.55 MiB app RSS at that same sample.

Initial think time delayed the full socket count; the 500k repeat sampled every connection live over 51.56 seconds. The VM capture added timing logs and request counters; normal 240k captures had failed latency limits. These results predate the final dependency refresh, and five-minute VM contest confirmation remains pending.

### Keep HTTP state only while a connection needs it

Most connections are idle between requests. Keeping a parser, read/write buffers and a scheduled task for every open socket exhausted memory. I patched [Hyper](https://github.com/hyperium/hyper/compare/master...mjc:hyper:benchmark-patches), the HTTP implementation underneath Axum, to return the still-open socket after a response finishes. The server can then release the HTTP state while preserving the connection. Partial requests, pipelined input and unfinished responses retain the state they still need.

Idle sockets share one Linux event watcher, which reports sockets with activity instead of making the server scan every connection. Its watches stay installed between requests, avoiding repeated kernel setup calls. HTTP work is limited to 8,192 active connections so a burst cannot allocate full request state for every socket at once. Each active connection has its own allowance for work before yielding back to the event loop, avoiding the starvation seen when the whole active set shared one allowance.

Tokio is the runtime that schedules asynchronous work and waits for network activity. The server registers an active socket with it only when a read or write cannot proceed immediately. Waiting for SQL alone therefore avoids that extra registration and its storage. Before returning a socket to idle, remembered notifications and a nonblocking read check prevent arriving input from being missed.

### Serialize rows without building a second set of posts

A conventional feed response first creates a list of post objects, copies their text fields, then walks the list again to encode JSON. This writer instead uses text directly from each SQLite row while the row is valid. Fixed field names and punctuation are written straight into the output; serde_json, the JSON encoder, handles the actual values and string escaping. That removes the intermediate list and string copies.

Each response starts with a buffer sized from the previous response's capacity, reducing repeated allocation and copying as it grows. Once encoded, the same allocation becomes the HTTP response body. Headers and body can be sent together from their existing buffers without copying them into a combined buffer. Hyper's body queue initially reserves only one entry because these responses contain one data buffer.

### Avoid extra request objects

- Post input is decoded directly into the field the handler needs, without a general JSON object containing copied values. Unescaped text uses a slice of the received bytes; escaped text reuses the decoder's allocation. Trimming selects a smaller slice instead of copying the text again.
- JWT decoding reads the required claims directly. A like validates the username without keeping a copied string that it will discard; post creation keeps it for the response. Signatures are checked on every request.
- Request headers are cleared after use, and the allocated table is reused for response headers. Hyper recycles that table after encoding, avoiding another allocation for the next response.
- The five routes are matched directly, avoiding the general router and the adapter between its service interface and Hyper. Paths refer to the existing request text; percent-encoded IDs are decoded as they are parsed, without creating another string. Only post creation uses Axum's machinery to collect and limit request-body bytes. Other routes and responses avoid body wrappers that need their own allocation. Dispatch also returns the handler's asynchronous operation directly, avoiding an extra wrapper that would retain more state in every active request.

### Reuse small HTTP allocations without retaining large ones

Hyper normally starts reads with an 8 KiB buffer. The patches start at 1 KiB, first reading into a temporary buffer that needs no separate allocation. Reusable heap storage is acquired when bytes actually arrive. Larger input can still grow. Handler storage and output-header buffers are also allocated only when needed, reducing memory reserved before there is work to do.

Read buffers, write-header buffers and header tables return to per-thread pools for reuse. Each pool holds at most 128 items, discarding buffers above 8 KiB and header tables with capacity above 32. These limits keep an unusually large request from permanently enlarging the pool. The read path tracks the original allocation because a tiny slice can otherwise keep a much larger allocation alive. Server-only builds remove Hyper's per-connection header cache and share the pooled tables instead. Pools survive periods with no active HTTP sessions so the next request can reuse them.

### Share database setup and commit costs

SQL runs on its own thread because a blocking database call on the HTTP event loop would stop unrelated connections from making progress. The SQL thread collects up to 1,024 requests, stopping when full or 1 ms after the first arrival. This gives nearby requests a chance to share transaction and commit costs while limiting the collection delay.

Consecutive reads share transaction setup. A write starts a mixed batch processed in queue order, so later reads see preceding writes. Each write has a savepoint, a rollback boundary that lets one failed write be undone without discarding the others. Replies wait for the group commit. Every request still runs its own SQL. Completion arrays are reused and only the current batch's entries are visited, avoiding initialization and scans of all 1,024 slots for small batches. Queue space is reserved before creating the reply channel so waiting requests do not allocate that channel prematurely.

Queries and transaction-control statements are prepared once, avoiding repeated SQL compilation. Long-lived statements are kept out of SQLite's small-allocation reserve, leaving that reserve available for temporary work. Each connection has one owning thread, so it does not need a lock around every operation. Disabling optional global page-cache management also avoids a shared cache-group lock. Batch deadlines use the SQL thread's existing sleep/wake mechanism instead of creating another asynchronous runtime.

Post creation uses `INSERT RETURNING` to get the new ID and timestamp from the insert, then combines them with the already validated body and username. It does not read the new row back. Successful likes rely on SQLite's foreign-key check to verify the post exists; extra existence queries are needed only for duplicates and failures.

### Reduce feed-query work without caching answers

The feed first selects the latest 20 post IDs. When those IDs occupy a small range, grouped range queries count likes and fetch the joined posts through the existing indexes, replacing repeated per-post lookups. Fixed arrays hold IDs, counts and serialized row positions, avoiding a heap-allocated lookup map. Row segments are copied into the required timestamp/ID order. Sparse or unsuitable ranges fall back to the original query. Each request uses current transaction data, with no token, post or query-result cache. The schema and indexes are unchanged.

### Keep checkpoint work away from sustained traffic

A checkpoint copies committed changes from the write-ahead log (WAL) into the database. Doing that storage work during a busy batch can stall requests. A separate connection starts the checkpoint after a full interval without SQL batch activity, and remembers when it has caught up so it does not repeatedly checkpoint an unchanged log. New traffic can still arrive during a checkpoint, and the WAL can grow during continuous load.

SQLite discards unused WAL capacity when the log safely resets. Later writes then extend the file, avoiding reads of cold old blocks needed for partial overwrites. Read transactions end before network responses are sent, so a slow client cannot keep a database snapshot open and prevent checkpoint progress.

SQLite's `unix-excl` backend keeps the temporary index used to locate WAL pages in process memory, avoiding stalls when updating its shared file on disk. The database and WAL remain on disk with NORMAL synchronization, and write success still waits for commit. The server needs exclusive database access.

### Leave memory for sockets and request bursts

Heap inspection found freed Rust allocations still occupying resident memory. Jemalloc, the replacement allocator, releases unused memory in the background. SQLite keeps its own system-allocator behavior. A small [Tokio patch](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/compare/master...mjc:tokio:benchmark-patches) reserves 64 KiB for the runtime's queue of ready work at startup. This avoids growing a long-lived queue among temporary connection allocations; it can still grow if needed. The allocation timing and retained capacity were verified; its separate throughput effect was not measured.

SQLite's page-cache target is 32 MiB to leave room for kernel socket storage and temporary request state. The SQL cache can otherwise consume memory needed to survive a request burst even when the idle connections fit.

title: Add ailang-native-2paws (AILANG, native SQLite, direct on :80)
body:
## What this is

A submission in **AILANG**, a language designed for AI-assisted systems programming. It has its own HTTP/1.1 event loop and a native memory-mapped, WAL-mode SQLite reader/writer (no `libsqlite3`, no shared libraries), and serves **directly** on `$HOST:$PORT` with no Nginx. JWT HS256 is verified on every authenticated request. Writes use group commit, and every response waits for its commit.

Folder: `submissions/ailang-native-2paws/`. It follows the layout in the README: `install.sh`, `build.sh`, `start.sh`, `README.md`, source, `.gitignore`.

## How it was built (please read)

This was **written entirely by AI under human direction**. Sean Collins set the goals and design direction, ran the benchmarks and decided what to keep. The AI wrote the server and the libraries and ran the tests. The README says this too. The folder `triumvirate-engineering/` describes the working method used (three AI roles that review each other's work). It is documentation only and is not part of the server.

The goal is a working reference for people using AILANG. We are fine with either outcome, accepted or not.

## Things you should know

1. **Rule 10 exception: a bundled compiler binary.** AILANG's compiler is self-hosting, so it cannot be built from a package or source tarball. The folder includes `compiler/ailang-opt11.x` (sha256 `eb705f6e60ece1bca1c1e8d3103b1a65be162b6fc63c690d85e1675f2efca407`), an optimizing build the server needs. The compiler published at AiLang-Author/Ailang-Self-Hosting- does not yet have the `Crc32String` that `Library.Hash` uses. An update that publishes the optimizer is coming. If a bundled binary is not acceptable, please decline and I will resubmit once the compiler is published. The server binary itself is built by `build.sh` and not committed. The compiler binary belongs to the AILANG project and is not covered by this repo's MIT license.
2. **License.** The source files are released under this repository's MIT license, per the submission terms.
3. **Local results are not official.** They come from an AMD FX-8320 (2012 Bulldozer family, 3.7 GHz) with the server pinned to one core, not a DigitalOcean droplet and not k6 (k6 runs out of memory above ~60k users there). High-concurrency runs used the C load generator from `c-iouring-raoz` with the same user loop as `bench/load.js`. On that machine: 5-minute holds **pass at 120,000 users** (p95 10.4 ms, p99 91 ms, 0 errors) and fail at 150,000. The single-core `GET /feed` comparison on the same machine was 19.5k req/s for this server against 2.9k for the FastAPI submission. Details are in the README. Treat the official benchmark as the real number.

## Testing

- `bash test/run.sh submissions/ailang-native-2paws` passes **42/42** locally from a clean build with the bundled compiler.
- `install.sh` is intentionally empty (nothing to install).

title: Add java-micronaut-Clickin submission (Java 25, Micronaut, JDBC + SQLite)
body:
Adds `submissions/java-micronaut-Clickin/`: Java 25 with Micronaut's standard HTTP stack and `sqlite-jdbc`, tuned for one vCPU **inside the framework** (no custom HTTP parser, no raw socket server, no FFM binding).

| | |
|---|---|
| Language / runtime | Java 25 — Eclipse Temurin `25.0.2+10`, SHA-256 verified by `install.sh` |
| Framework | Micronaut 5.2.15 (Platform 5.2.2) on Netty 4.2.19.Final, portable `nio` transport |
| Database / driver | SQLite via `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` 3.53.4.0 (**JDBC**) |
| JSON | SQLite renders every feed and post read (`json_object`). Everything else uses Micronaut Serialization with **build-time bean introspection** (no runtime reflection, no `jackson-databind`) |
| JWT | Hand-written HS256 check on the JDK's `Mac` (HmacSHA256): verified on every authenticated request, `alg` must be `HS256`, constant-time signature comparison (`MessageDigest.isEqual`), fresh `exp`/`sub`/`username` checks. No verification cache |
| **Nginx or direct** | **Direct** on `HOST:PORT` (`0.0.0.0:80` on the benchmark VM) |

**`test/run.sh` → 42/42** on a fresh seed database. Dependencies are pinned in `gradle.lockfile`; the Gradle wrapper is checksum-verified.

### Approach

- **Event loop & DB owner:** One Netty `nio` event loop handles HTTP parsing, routing, JWT verification and validation. One `db-owner` thread owns a single SQLite connection with all statements prepared at startup, so JDBC never blocks the event loop.
- **Opportunistic group commit:** The DB owner drains up to 256 queued operations per pass and executes batches containing writes inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE … COMMIT`. Every response in the batch is completed only after `COMMIT` succeeds (WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`), guaranteeing durable writes prior to 201 responses. Failed batches roll back and fail with 500; writes are never retried.
- **Zero-overhead read responses:** Feed and single-post reads (~92% of traffic) return raw UTF-8 `BLOB` bytes built directly by SQLite, bypassing row-mapping and re-serialization.
- **Memory & GC:** Tuned for the 1 vCPU / 2 GB constraint with Serial GC and a fixed 384 MB young generation (`-Xms768m -Xmx768m -Xmn384m -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=3 -XX:MetaspaceSize=64m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=64m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch`), preventing ramp-up survivor overflows and keeping GC pauses short under high connection concurrency.

### Verification

- **Tests:** `install.sh` → `build.sh` (JUnit covering batch rollbacks, lost-commit recovery, queue-overflow 503s) → `test/run.sh` → **42/42**. Supplemental HTTP checks in `checks/` verify Unicode handling, concurrent likes/creates, and write-visibility. `PRAGMA integrity_check` is `ok` and `foreign_key_check` is empty after every run.
- **Preliminary Load Benchmarks (Self-run):** Tested on DigitalOcean `s-1vcpu-2gb` droplets using the README search protocol (1,000-VU warm-up, doubling from 2,500, narrowing to 250, 5-minute confirmation hold).
  - With `LimitNOFILE=131072`: **84,500 VUs confirmed** (p99 218 ms, 0% errors, 92% CPU). That is at the edge (p99 swings between 0.2 s and 1.9 s from 82.5k up); a comfortable level is about **70,000 VUs** (p99 134–216 ms, 86–87% CPU).
  - With default limit (`65,535` FDs): **64,000 VUs confirmed** (p99 283 ms, 0% errors, 82% CPU).
  - HotSpot JIT beat GraalVM Native Image (PGO and plain) at 70,000 VUs on CPU per request and tail latency (116–118 µs vs 121–130 µs; p99 134–216 ms vs ~555 ms), so the submission runs on HotSpot.
  *(Details and full measurement tables are in the submission README.)*

### Disclosures

Built with AI pair programming (Claude Code). Commits carry `Co-Authored-By` trailers.

title: Add asm-epoll-umitaltintas submission (x86-64 NASM, epoll, SQLite; direct on :80)
body:
A hand-written **x86-64 assembly** server (NASM, Linux): epoll event loop, HTTP/1.1 parser, router, strict RFC 8259 JSON reader, JSON writer, base64url, SHA-256/HMAC and JWT verification. SQLite 3.50.4 (pinned amalgamation, sha256-checked) is the only C code. libc is linked only because SQLite needs it, and all socket I/O uses raw syscalls.

- **Nginx or direct:** direct on `HOST:PORT`.
- **Architecture:** one thread and one SQLite connection. Each epoll batch is processed in four steps: handle every ready request; run the writes inside one transaction (group commit); build all responses into one arena; **COMMIT, then send**. A 201 always means the row is committed.
- **The optimization that mattered most:** under constant writes, a background PASSIVE checkpoint never reaches the end of the WAL, so SQLite never rewinds it. Locally the WAL grew to 247 MB in 90 s and `/feed` slowed from 37 µs to 123 µs. Now a background thread does the bulk copy and fsync, and the event loop finishes the last frames right after sending a batch. The WAL stays around 16 MB.
- Details, trade-offs and local numbers are in the [README](submissions/asm-epoll-umitaltintas/README.md).

- **Keep-alive budget:** with `LimitNOFILE=65535` and one fd per keep-alive client, the 65,536th client can't connect. And a Linux client has only ~28k local ports per server address by default, so a single untuned machine running more users than that can't connect at all while each user holds a keep-alive connection. So keep-alive has two budgets: 60,000 connections in total and 20,000 per client address. New connections past either get `Connection: close`; existing ones stay. Closing responses go out with `MSG_MORE` and the socket is closed right after, so the FIN rides on the last data segment and `TIME_WAIT` stays on the server, not on the client's ports. On `EMFILE` the listen socket leaves epoll until a connection closes. New connections are also accepted every 128 events within a batch, so the 4096-entry accept queue doesn't overflow.

**Local results, native x86-64:** an x86-64 KVM server (AMD EPYC-Milan, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8), the server pinned to one vCPU with 2 GiB and `nofile=65535`, database on local disk. The load came from a Go re-implementation of `bench/load.js` with the same loop and think times: four processes on other vCPUs, each from its own loopback address. No network card was in between. 90 s ramp, 2 min hold.

| VUs | p95 | p99 | errors | server CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 96,000 | 1.1 ms | ~45 ms | 0% | 55% |
| 128,000 | ~16 ms | ~55 ms | 0% | 74% |
| 160,000 | ~31 ms | ~65 ms | 0% | 89% |
| 192,000 | ~55 ms | ~87 ms | 0% | 95% |

Under Rosetta on an Apple Silicon Mac (5 min holds), 96k passed and 112k was CPU-bound; details are in the README.

From **one client address with the default port range**, 40k users went from 16% connect errors (all client-side) to 0 errors; 48k pass with p99 42 ms. Above ~50k from one address my load generator ran out of CPU, so I couldn't measure further.

Before the keep-alive cap, everything above about 64k VUs failed. I also tried one fd table per thread (`unshare(CLONE_FILES)` + `SO_REUSEPORT`). It held 112k keep-alive connections, but it was no faster and forced SQLite into exclusive locking, so I left it out; the README explains why. These numbers only compare changes to this code; they are not a prediction for the droplet.

`test/run.sh` passes 42/42 in a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container (install.sh as root, build and test as a normal user).

title: Add python-stdlib-shawal-mbalire submission
body:
Adds `submissions/python-stdlib-shawal-mbalire/`: the same five endpoints on **CPython 3.15 and the standard library only**, served **direct** on `0.0.0.0:80`. No third-party packages, no `requirements.txt`.

**Built from source on the box** (rule 10): `build.sh` downloads python.org's CPython 3.15.0 and sqlite.org's SQLite 3.53.1, checks each against a pinned SHA-256, and compiles them with clang 19 from Ubuntu (PGO + ThinLTO, the tail-call interpreter). `start.sh` runs the server from a venv on that interpreter. The venv has no pip and no packages. It's the author's second entry, next to #41 (FastAPI + Granian), and asks how close plain CPython can get to #84 (PyPy + raw epoll).

## Highlights

- **A hand-written `select.epoll` loop nested in the standard `asyncio` loop** (no uvloop). asyncio watches one descriptor, the epoll instance, and the server reads and writes every ready socket with `os.read`/`os.write`. There is no transport, protocol object or scheduled callback per connection. Timers, the group commit and the WAL checkpoint stay on asyncio.
- **A hand-written HTTP/1.1 parser** (`bytes.find`/`split`) with keep-alive, pipelining, `Content-Length` bodies, and 400/413/431 on bad input. Why not `http.server`: it starts one thread per connection, and every user here holds one, so 40k+ users would mean 40k+ threads in 1.75 GiB.
- **Requests run without Tasks.** Each workflow coroutine is driven by hand: a read finishes inside its read event, and a write suspends on its group commit's future.
- **SQLite renders every response** (`json_object` / `group_concat`); Python only joins byte strings. The standard `json` module only decodes request bodies and JWT parts.
- **Group commit**: writes in one loop pass share a `COMMIT`, and every response waits for its commit. One `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` WAL connection, `synchronous=NORMAL`, a passive checkpoint every second.
- **TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT** (as in #84): a connection is accepted, read and answered in one pass.
- **Descriptor guard** (as in #41): past ~61k open TCP sockets (from `/proc/self/net/sockstat`), responses carry `Connection: close`. Accepting also pauses 64 descriptors short of the limit, so the server never hits EMFILE.
- JWT HS256 is verified by hand (`hmac`) on every request; no caching across requests.

## Verification

- `test/run.sh`: **42/42 pass** in a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container, with `install.sh` and `build.sh` (which compiles Python). 78 unit tests (stdlib `unittest`) pass.
- Build time: install + build + start + tests took 2 min 46 s on 8 CPUs. On a 1-vCPU droplet the compile will take much longer (not measured); `start.sh` is healthy within seconds.

## Results (not a droplet score)

These were measured on python-build-standalone's CPython 3.15.0 (same version and compiler features), before `build.sh` compiled it from source; a comparison of the two builds is running and will be added here.

Same bench as #41: `just bench linux` on an Apple M-series machine (faster cores than a droplet vCPU). The server gets CPU 0, 1792 MiB, no swap and nofile 65535, and four containers run PR #14's C load generator over a Docker bridge (not loopback).

**Limit search, 2-minute holds** (2026-10-17). The 5-minute holds the challenge requires haven't been run yet, so treat these as an upper bound:

| Users | Pass | server CPU µs/request | CPU 0 busy | p95 | p99 | errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 140,000 | yes | 56.0 | 66% | 8.5 ms | 24 ms | 0 |
| 170,000 | yes | 58.8 | 84% | 28.7 ms | 72 ms | 0 |
| 180,000 | yes | 60.4 | 92% | 105 ms | 207 ms | 0 |
| 190,000 | no | 67.0 | 79% | 813 ms | 13.5 s | 0.13% |

(At 190k the load generator itself fell 6.3 s behind.)

**130,000 users, alternating runs** (3 rounds, 120 s hold, 2026-10-16):

| Entry | Pass | server CPU µs/request | CPU 0 busy | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #84 PyPy + raw epoll | 3/3 | 51.1–54.9 (52.7) | 57% | 14–17 ms |
| **this entry** | **3/3** | **57.4–59.5 (58.7)** | 64% | 24–63 ms |
| this entry on `asyncio.Protocol` + `loop.create_server` | 2/3 | 75.9–85.0 (79.0) | 84% | 41 ms – 4.0 s |

In a separate alternating run at 130k, #41 (FastAPI + Granian) cost 62.1–63.5 µs per request. The README has the method and details.

Only `submissions/python-stdlib-shawal-mbalire/` is added.

title: Add Nim submission: direct HTTP/1.1 + in-process SQLite (io_uring networking)
body:
Adds `submissions/nim-io_uring-NioHast/`.

## Summary

A direct HTTP/1.1 server in Nim 2.2.12, compiled to C, with in-process SQLite 3.54.0. The server binds directly, owns its database, and uses one io_uring request loop, one SQLite connection, and one inline WAL checkpoint path.

- **Toolchain:** Nim 2.2.12, pinned and sha256-verified by `install.sh`.
- **Networking:** io_uring with multishot accept, direct fixed-slot accept, multishot recv, and a registered provided-buffer ring. The pool defaults to 256 x 8 KiB; `IOURING_BUFS` overrides it.
- **Database:** SQLite 3.54.0 amalgamation, pinned and sha256-verified, compiled in-tree by `build.sh`. There is no system `libsqlite3` dependency.
- **Auth:** HS256 JWT via HMAC-SHA256 with vendored nimcrypto 0.7.3.

## Design and optimizations

- **Direct HTTP and one request thread:** no reverse proxy, framework, worker pool, or per-request thread handoff.
- **One SQLite connection:** `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, `SQLITE_THREADSAFE=0`, `synchronous=NORMAL`, WAL, `wal_autocheckpoint=0`, `journal_size_limit=64 MiB`, `mmap_size=1 GiB`, `cache_size=-64`.
- **Inline checkpoint:** the WAL hook records the frame count. At the process-wide pass boundary, after the pass COMMIT and `endRead`, the single connection runs one `SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART` when the count is at least 4096 frames. `SQLITE_BUSY` leaves the count for the next pass and never spins. WAL stays around 16 MiB.
- **Durable group commit:** writes in one event-loop pass share a transaction, and responses wait for the COMMIT.
- **Feed read path:** top-20 ids through the `created_at` index, likes in the id window, then a rowid range (`id BETWEEN ? AND ?`, no `ORDER BY` or `INDEXED BY`) with in-memory slot reassembly.
- **JSON:** reusable `feedScratch`; segments are copied directly into the response with `copyMem`. No per-feed or per-row temporary string.
- **io_uring:** multishot accept and recv, direct fixed-slot accept, provided buffers, CQ headroom, completion batching, fixed-file close.
- **HTTP, JSON, auth:** borrowed request spans, SSE2 escaping, two-digit integer formatting, fixed stack JWT scratch.
- **Memory:** 80-byte `Conn`, lazy slots, pooled output buffers, no receive buffer on idle connections, slot generations, idle sweep.
- **Build:** `BUILD_VARIANT=danger` by default (`-d:danger`), `PGO=1` by default, LTO, `-march=native`, `-fno-semantic-interposition`, `-fno-plt`, `--mm:arc`, `--threads:off`; SQLite `THREADSAFE=0` and `HAVE_FDATASYNC=1`. `BUILD_VARIANT=control` is an opt-in checked `-d:release` build.

## Measured local results

These are same-session local measurements on a WSL2 box with four vCPUs. The server and load generator share the host over loopback, so these are not organiser numbers.

64,000 paced mixed connections, four-repetition mean:

| Metric | Result |
|---|---:|
| Throughput | about 6,800 req/s |
| CPU | 62.2% of one core |
| User CPU | 18.25% |
| System CPU | 43.95% |
| p99 | 41-229 ms (median about 86 ms) |
| RSS | 142.8 MiB |
| WAL max | 16.2 MiB |
| Errors | 0 |

The p99 high end is a pass-boundary checkpoint stall. Every run stayed below the 1 s p99 threshold with zero errors.

k6 `bench/load.js`, 5,000 VUs, 30 s ramp + 120 s hold:

| Metric | Result |
|---|---:|
| CPU | 8.3% of one core |
| User CPU | 3.0% |
| System CPU | 5.25% |
| p95 | 4.46 ms |
| p99 | 14.1 ms |
| Errors | 0 |

The local load generator is co-located with the server. It cannot certify a maximum user count; that requires a separate load-generator machine.

## Rules Compliance

- SQLite only, in-process; no external database or cache (Rule 2).
- No caching across requests; every JWT is verified per request (Rule 5).
- Durable before responding, `synchronous=NORMAL`, never `OFF` (Rule 6).
- No hard-coded responses and no benchmark detection (Rule 7).
- Direct bind, no reverse proxy required (Rule 9).
- Built from source with pinned dependencies, no prebuilt binary shipped (Rule 10).
- The server does not tune kernel parameters or pin itself; only in-process settings are used (Rule 11).
- The shipping `-d:danger` build removes Nim runtime bounds/overflow/range checks and `assert`; the 42-check suite and 64k load test pass, and malformed-input fuzzing is advisable.
- The commit-failure harness is not applicable to the single-connection `EXCLUSIVE` design; the 42-check suite is the CI gate, and durability was verified with a 3,000-post SIGTERM/reopen check.

## Dependencies

Runtime: glibc only. Build: pinned downloads (Nim 2.2.12, SQLite 3.54.0, nimcrypto 0.7.3, all sha256-verified) plus standard Ubuntu tools. There are no Nimble packages.

## Docs

`README.md` and `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, `docs/DEPENDENCIES.md`, and `docs/OPTIMIZATIONS.md`.

## Limitations

- Local measurements share one box with the load generator. They are not the organiser numbers.
- The target is a 1 vCPU / 2 GB droplet. A true maximum-user score requires a separate load generator.
- `-d:danger` removes Nim runtime checks. The 42-check suite and 64k test pass, but fuzzing is advisable.
- The commit-failure harness uses a second SQLite connection and is not applicable to the `EXCLUSIVE` single-connection design.
- WAL is on disk and is not part of process RSS.

MIT, under the repository license.

title: Add c-libco-ssmurfgg04-gif submission (C, libco coroutines, SQLite, direct on :80)
body:
A second engine for the same handler layers as my c-iouring submission (#112): the HTTP parsing, JWT, JSON and SQLite code are byte-identical files; the connection layer is replaced by [Tencent libco](https://github.com/Tencent/libco), the coroutine library that runs WeChat backend.

## What it is

- `LIBCO_PROCS` processes (default: 1 on small-RAM boxes like the droplet, 2 otherwise), each with its own `SO_REUSEPORT` listener and one single-threaded libco event loop
- one coroutine per connection from an idle pool that grows on demand, shared stacks (128 x 128KB), so stack memory is O(stacks) not O(connections)
- per-connection code is straight-line: `co_poll(POLLIN)` -> `read` -> route -> `write` (poll `POLLOUT` on EAGAIN). No connection state machine, no buffer rings, no manual backpressure bookkeeping
- the DB layer needs no locks by construction: coroutines are cooperative and never yield inside a transaction, so one SQLite connection per process is serialized without a mutex, and every transaction commits before its responses are sent (same ordering guarantee as group commit). Sibling processes share the db via WAL, `busy_timeout` 1000ms, passive checkpoint every 5s
- direct on :80 (no Nginx)

## Numbers

- 42/42 conformance (local, `test/run.sh`)
- On our bench rig (server pinned to 2 cores, a C load generator mirroring `bench/load.js`): 100k VUs PASS avg 0.4ms p99 5ms; 250k VUs PASS avg 10.4ms p95 100ms, zero failed requests. Beyond ~262k connections that rig itself stops delivering connections (a canned-response sink with no app logic fails identically), so 250k is its ceiling
- memory: ~0.5KB per idle connection coroutine (see the libco notes below)

## Vendored libco notes (two small documented patches)

- hook fd map widened 102400 -> 1048576: stock libco silently degrades its syscall hooks past 102400 fds per process
- `aSpec[1024]` slimmed to `[8]`: 8KB per coroutine of routine-specific storage this server never uses

Both are commented in place. libco is Apache 2.0 (license vendored).

title: Add java-springboot-bogdan-blaj submission (Java 25, Spring Boot 4 + raw Netty epoll, SQLite via FFM, direct on :80)
body:
Adds a Java implementation of all five endpoints. Spring Boot 4.1.1 (no web starter) hosts a raw Netty 4.2.17 epoll
server on one event loop; SQLite 3.53.4 is built from the official amalgamation by `build.sh` and called inline on
that loop through the Java FFM API (no JDBC). Direct mode on `0.0.0.0:80`, no Nginx.

How it follows the rules:

- Every request reads SQLite while it is served. Response JSON is built by SQLite (`json_object`), statements are
  prepared once, nothing is cached across requests, and every JWT signature is verified (HS256, constant-time compare).
- WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`. Writes are group-committed: one transaction per event-loop pass, and every response
  from that pass is held until `COMMIT` returns, so a 201 always means committed. A failed commit turns that pass's
  responses into 500.
- Fixed schema, no kernel tuning, configured only by the SPEC env vars. Pinned JDK, Maven, Spring Boot, Netty and
  SQLite (checksummed downloads); no prebuilt binaries are committed.

Main optimizations (details in the README):

- One thread does everything (1 vCPU): parse, JWT, SQLite, respond, commit, checkpoint.
- `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` and manual `RESTART` checkpoints at 1,000 WAL frames from a `wal_hook`, run after
  responses are flushed. Larger thresholds gave a worse p99 locally.
- The feed steps 20 `json_object` rows over `posts_created_at_id_idx` (no sort), and the body is copied once into a
  pooled direct buffer.
- No per-request allocation in our code: byte-level JWT and strict JSON body parsing with reused scratch buffers.
- Fixed 640 MiB pre-touched heap with Serial GC, compact object headers.
- Connection guard sized from the descriptor limit: above `min(65000, nofile - reserve)` open connections (65,000 under
  `nofile=65535`), responses carry `Connection: close`, so `accept()` never runs out of descriptors. Up to 65,000
  users keep their connection; users above that reconnect for the next request.

Validation:

- `test/run.sh`: 42/42 on Linux arm64 and 42/42 on Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04 amd64 container under Rosetta, clean
  `install.sh` + `test/run.sh`; healthy about 5 s after `start.sh` under emulation, about 3 s natively).
- 39 additional HTTP checks (pipelining, chunked bodies, 100-continue, 413/400, keep-alive reuse after 66 s idle).
- Crash durability: 200/200 acknowledged creates and likes survived SIGKILL and restart.
- Descriptor pressure: with `nofile=512`, connections above the guard are served and closed, and keep-alive resumes
  once pressure ends.
- 64,000 idle keep-alive connections held and reused: about 1.6 KiB of heap per connection.
- Official `bench/load.js` with k6 2.3.0, unchanged, 5,000 users (30 s ramp, 3 min hold): 115,485 requests,
  0 failed, p95 1.4 ms, p99 3.8 ms, server CPU 8.4%.
- Users above the keep-alive cap: same k6 run with the cap at 1,666 (two thirds of users reconnect per request)
  and at 4,250: about 575k requests including ~40k likes and ~5k creates, 0 failures, p95/p99 unchanged, about
  12-37 µs of extra CPU per reconnect.
- Start conditions like the service: non-root, `nofile=65535`, ambient `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `PORT=80`: healthy
  in about 3.5 s and 42/42 on port 80. Without the capability the bind fails with EACCES and the process exits 1.

Local capacity runs (Docker Desktop on Apple Silicon, linux/arm64; server on 1 CPU, 2 GB without swap,
`nofile=65535`, unchanged `start.sh`, fresh seed per run). k6 needs ~0.33 MiB per user, so these use a small C
replay of `bench/load.js` (same loop, think times, one keep-alive connection per user, reconnect on
`Connection: close`, k6-style timing) on 4 client containers; it matched k6 at 5,000 users. 60 s ramp + 5 min hold:

| Users | p95 | p99 | Failed requests (hold) | req/s | Server CPU | cgroup memory peak |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64,000 | 4.8 ms | 23 ms | 0 of 2.03M | 6,772 | 38% | 1,581 MiB |
| 65,000 | 5.6 ms | 24 ms | 0 of 2.06M | 6,876 | 39% | 1,579 MiB |
| 70,000 | 7.8 ms | 46 ms | 0 of 2.22M | 7,409 | 43% | 1,496 MiB |
| 80,000 | 15 ms | 151 ms | 0 of 2.54M | 8,463 | 51% | 1,584 MiB |

Latencies are for the 5 min hold. Up to 65,000 users every user keeps one connection for the whole run. Above that,
responses carry `Connection: close` and those users reconnect (about 5k reconnects per 10 s at 70k, 16k at 80k);
open connections stay at about 65,000 and no request fails. No OOM, no listen drops; Java RSS stays under 930 MB and
the memory peak includes about 510 MiB of reclaimable database page cache. These are local relative numbers, not the
x86_64 droplet score.

Local numbers (Docker Desktop on Apple Silicon, linux/arm64, server on 1 CPU with 2 GB; relative only, not the
x86_64 droplet): wrk with 64 connections, mixed traffic 57.1k req/s at 14.6 µs CPU per request; feed only 48.6k req/s.

Only `submissions/java-springboot-bogdan-blaj/` is changed.

title: zig io-uring marler8997
body:
Add zig-iouring-marler8997 (Zig 0.17 std.Io on io_uring fibers, SQLite, direct on :80)

A Zig 0.17 server whose code reads like ordinary blocking code, written against Zig's new `std.Io` interface: accept, read a request, handle it, write the response, one `Io.Group` task per connection. It is still fully asynchronous. Under it is our own `Io` ([`src/UringIo.zig`](submissions/zig-iouring-marler8997/src/UringIo.zig)): one thread, one io_uring, and a fiber per connection. Through [zig-staticio](https://github.com/marler8997/zig-staticio), every `std.Io` call becomes a direct call into it, with no vtable.

- **Direct** on `0.0.0.0:80`, no Nginx.
- **About 300 bytes per idle connection.** A waiting connection's stack is packed to about 160 bytes and its pages go back to the kernel.
- Group commit, WAL checkpoints on an idle-priority thread, the feed served with range scans, and hand-written HTTP, JSON and JWT.
- SQLite 3.54.1 is the only C code. Zig and every dependency are pinned by hash.

**Local measurements:** a Ryzen 9 5950X with the server pinned to one core. The load comes from a load generator that follows `bench/load.js`, included as `zig build loadgen`. At 64,000 users with a 120 s hold: 0 failed requests, p99 1.3 ms, 16.1% CPU and 24.2 MB RSS. These are unofficial; the droplet will differ.

`test/run.sh` passes 42/42, and `zig build test` runs the unit tests. The README has the design and the measurements behind each optimization.

title: submission: lua-lunet-simbo1905
body:
The Feed API in plain Lua on [lunet](https://github.com/lua-lunet/lunet) — a libuv + LuaJIT coroutine runtime. Application logic only: `server.lua` plus `app/` (posts, auth, health, config, db). Routing, HTTP/1.1 framing (persist-by-default keep-alive), JWT and the fixed-shape render helpers ride on the runtime's own extensions — `lunet.http_router`, `lunet.http_context`, `lunet.http`, `lunet.security`, `lunet.jsonic`.

**Runtime:** pinned `v0.14.1` release archive install (digest-checked in `build.sh`), the same way a Node submission installs Node. No compiler, no toolchain: `install.sh` needs apt packages only.

**Shape:** behind the provided nginx on `127.0.0.1:3000`; keep-alive honored in-process (responses persist by default; a request declaring `Connection: close` is answered and the connection stops being served). SQLite in WAL via the bundled driver's `(rw, ro)` split with explicit handles — `query_ro` (read-only connection, inline on the loop, fast reads only), `query` (read-write worker pool, writes that RETURN), `exec` (write results); `synchronous=NORMAL` through the driver's open contract; JWTs verified fresh per request through `lunet.security`'s RFC-7518 HS256 decoder; responses rendered in the byte-exact shapes the spec mandates. `start.sh` mirrors the harness's `LimitNOFILE=65535` grant and runs one background thread (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1`).

**Verified:** the SPEC contract matrix green locally (macOS) and on a 1 vCPU / 2 GiB linux-arm64 VM (the release archive for each platform), plus the repo's `test submissions` CI green on the default branch.

**Benchmark** (1 vCPU / 2 GiB, no swap, nothing tuned; load generator sharing the same core — harder than the scored setup): 5-minute hold at 2,500 VUs — **checks 100.00% (93,477 requests, 0 failed), p95 0.45 ms, p99 0.79 ms, peak RSS 16.9 MB**.

title: Add kotlin-trikeshed-jnorthrup submission (Kotlin 2.4.21, GraalVM 25.4, RelaxFactory one.xio NIO reactor, SQLite via FFM, direct on :80)
body:
Hi @arjaythedev, thank you for hosting the $12 Server Challenge. The spec, the 42-check harness and the load test made it a fun target to build against, and I appreciate you running the batches on the DigitalOcean droplet.

This PR adds `submissions/kotlin-trikeshed-jnorthrup/`: Kotlin 2.4.21 on Oracle GraalVM 25.4.4.1.1 (JDK 25) with no framework. It is RelaxFactory's `one.xio` NIO reactor on one thread, with SQLite 3.54.0 compiled by `build.sh` and called through `java.lang.foreign`. It serves directly on `HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=80` (no Nginx). The folder's README covers the optimizations and the reasons for each.

Files outside the folder:
- `.gitmodules`: git keeps submodule entries at the repo root. `trikeshed/TrikeShed` is jnorthrup/TrikeShed pinned at `17c7180dd` (tag `v2026.10.18`). A checkout without submodules also works, because `build.sh` fetches that recorded commit.
- 10 `.gitignore` lines: Gradle/Kotlin build directories and `.env`.

Local gate: in a fresh clone of this branch (`4ea331f`), the submodule directory started empty. `build.sh` fetched TrikeShed `17c7180dd` from GitHub, and `test/run.sh` reported `passed=42 failed=0` (macOS arm64).

Final measurements of each variant, all taken on my own machines (none on a droplet). Your batch run is the one that counts.

### HTTP, 64,000 users: Kali Linux x86_64 (WSL2, i7-6820HK)
Setup:
- Server: pinned to one CPU (taskset + cgroup cpuset), `cpu.max` of one CPU, `memory.max` 2 GiB, no swap.
- Client: the folder's Kotlin load generator (the `bench/load.js` workload) on CPUs 2-7.
- Run: 60 s ramp, then a 300 s hold with all users connected. Fresh JVM, no warmup.

| transport | date | hold req/s | server CPU per request | hold p50 / p95 / p99 / max (ms) | failed requests | load.js thresholds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `one.xio`, java.nio/epoll, one selector per transport state (the default) | 2026-10-18 | 6,732 | 69.9 µs | 55.3 / 100.4 / 122.9 / 176.6 | 0 | pass (full run including ramp: p95 100.4, p99 123.9, max 245.0 ms) |
| `TRANSPORT=ring` (optional), kernel io_uring via FFM | 2026-10-17 | 6,681 | 74.5 µs | 59.9 / 368.6 / 1,933.3 / 3,549.0 | 0 | fail (p99) |
| `TRANSPORT=ring` (optional), emulated ring | 2026-10-17 | 6,661 | 90.4 µs | 63.5 / 130.0 / 835.6 / 3,298.6 | 0 | fail (full-run p95 557.1, p99 4,456.4 ms) |

The two ring rows used a 1 GiB heap and 3 client source addresses. The `one.xio` row used the shipped `-Xms384m -Xmx384m` and 6 addresses; with 3 addresses, client port pressure stalled the ramp. The ring rows were not rerun.

### HTTP, 8,192 users: macOS arm64 (Apple M3 Pro), 2026-10-17
No CPU or memory cap; the client runs on the same host. 10 s ramp, 30 s hold. This Mac cannot reach 64,000 connections (16,384 fds and 16,384 ephemeral ports per address).
- `one.xio` (the single-selector build of that day): 785.7 req/s, p50 / p95 / p99 / max 26.6 / 66.6 / 385.0 / 786.5 ms, 0 failed requests.
- `TRANSPORT=ring`, emulated: 819.3 req/s, 29.4 / 87.0 / 835.6 / 1,278.1 ms, 330 connect failures (EADDRNOTAVAIL: ephemeral ports still held from the previous run).

### TrikeShed's I/O ring per runtime
Units: ops/s, where one op is a batch of 8 SQEs. Each cell gives NOP / 4 KiB write / 4 KiB read. Two harnesses ran: kotlinx-benchmark (JMH: 5 x 1 s warmup, 10 x 1 s measured), and the same loop in JMH's shape for the runtimes JMH cannot drive (native images). TrikeShed `cd43a2005` (`v2026.10.17.1`) unless noted.

Kali x86_64, kotlinx-benchmark:

| runtime | emulated ring | kernel io_uring |
|---|---|---|
| JVM (Graal JIT) | 12,067,755 / 68,018 / 76,315 | 428,113 / 14,077 / 123,420 |
| Node (Kotlin/JS) | 2,082,741 / 47,380 / 57,571 | 211,111 / 11,478 / 79,222 |
| Kotlin/Native linuxX64 | 892,204 / 66,117 / 77,224 | 268,352 / 14,060 / 114,582 |
| Kotlin/Wasm WASI (TrikeShed `ea6a4242f`, 2026-10-16) | 4,060,438 / 14,117 / 6,841 | not available |

Kali x86_64, loop harness:

| build | emulated ring | kernel io_uring |
|---|---|---|
| JVM JIT | 9,069,830 / 65,491 / 72,104 | 425,273 / 13,702 / 116,413 |
| JDK AOT cache | 7,240,046 / 66,180 / 77,287 | 388,863 / 14,156 / 119,913 |
| GraalVM native image (18.4 MB) | 4,424,235 / 57,106 / 65,934 | 383,935 / 14,039 / 106,411 |
| native image + PGO (13.0 MB) | 6,530,776 / 64,409 / 71,841 | 407,398 / 14,328 / 116,340 |
| static (nolibc) native image + PGO (13.1 MB) | 6,608,752 / 63,712 / 71,589 | 415,513 / 14,378 / 115,884 |

macOS arm64 (M3), emulated ring only (io_uring is Linux-only):

| runtime / build | harness | NOP / write / read |
|---|---|---|
| JVM (Graal JIT) | kotlinx-benchmark | 33,041,585 / 177,722 (±32%) / 252,234 |

### Cold-process file I/O, no warmup, 2026-10-17
One fresh process per case, with every iteration counted. Kali processes were limited to one CPU and 2 GiB. Each cell gives 4 KiB ops in batches of 64, NOP / WRITE / READ in ops/s:
- Kali JVM, kernel io_uring (FFM): 59,858 / 74,903 / 128,291

title: Add Go net/http + SQLite submission (go-nethttp-NaveedZahoorKhan)
body:
## Submission: `go-nethttp-NaveedZahoorKhan`

A feed API on SQLite tuned for the $12 box (1 vCPU, 2 GB), served **directly** (no Nginx).

### Stack
- **Go 1.24.4** (pinned in `install.sh`, SHA-256 verified), stdlib `net/http`, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive.
- **`github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3` v1.14.22** (cgo); the SQLite amalgamation is vendored, so the SQLite version is pinned by the driver, not the box. Dependencies are vendored — `build.sh` needs no network.
- **Direct mode**: binds `0.0.0.0:80` and handles keep-alive connections itself.

### Design
- **Reader pool over WAL** — N read-only connections (channel pool), each with pinned prepared statements (plan cache only, rule 5).
- **Batched row reader** — one added file in the vendored driver (`sqlite3_post5.go`) steps + reads all 5 post columns in a single cgo call, avoiding per-column crossings and `driver.Value` boxing. Feed read ~117 µs → ~36 µs locally; byte-identical output (golden tests pass).
- **Group-commit writer** — a single writer goroutine batches queued writes into one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE … COMMIT`; each request still blocks until its own commit returns (durable 201s, rule 6). No artificial batching delay.
- **Hand-rolled HS256 JWT** verification every request (no `encoding/json` on the hot path, nothing cached — rule 5).
- **Hand-written JSON output** in exact key order; manual id/body validation.
- **Pragmas**: WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`, 1 GB `mmap_size`, 16 MB page cache, `PRAGMA optimize`; `GOMEMLIMIT` caps the heap so memory stops co-limiting at scale.

### Correctness
Passes all 42 checks in `test/test.sh` on a fresh seed DB. (Run with `TZ=UTC` — the suite's "created_at is now" check mis-parses the timestamp as local time on non-UTC machines; the server stores true UTC and CI runs in UTC.)

### Self-measured capacity (indicative, not the official score)
In a container pinned to droplet limits (`--cpus=1 --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g`), k6 on a second container over a Docker bridge: passes **60k VUs** with 0 errors (p99 ~357 ms). Could not measure higher — the single load container exhausts ephemeral ports (~64k) before the server fails, so the real ceiling is bounded by the harness, not the code. Bottleneck is single-core CPU inside SQLite's cgo execution.

Nginx vs direct and all optimizations are detailed in the submission README.

body:
ran the full 6m30s profile (`1m` ramp up -> `5m` hold -> `30s` ramp down) across 32k, 64k, 96k, and 128k vus against the 500k posts / 2m likes seed db:

| vus | median (p50) | p95 | p99 | avg | server ram (vmrss / vmdata) | total reqs (req/s) | failed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 32k | 1.87 ms | 4.79 ms | 6.79 ms | 2.05 ms | 276.1 MiB / 3.5 MiB | 947,043 (2,419/s) | 0 (0%) |
| 64k | 2.56 ms | 6.17 ms | 8.52 ms | 2.76 ms | 275.8 MiB / 4.0 MiB | 1,171,535 (2,981/s) | 0 (0%) |
| 96k | 3.37 ms | 8.74 ms | 11.99 ms | 4.16 ms | 275.6 MiB / 3.6 MiB | 1,077,363 (2,737/s) | 0 (0%) |
| 128k | 4.18 ms | 10.63 ms | 14.56 ms | 5.23 ms | 276.7 MiB / 3.6 MiB | 1,080,310 (2,744/s) | 0 (0%) |

few notes on the numbers:
- actual private ram (`VmData`, `.bss` buffers + sqlite state) sits around 1.7 MiB at idle and peaks at 3.5-4.0 MiB under load. `VmRSS` shows ~276 MiB because `mmap_size = 1GB` maps the 263 MiB `feed.db` file into the address space from the os page cache (`buff/cache`).
- for 96k and 128k, the first 65,000 fds stay on persistent `keep-alive` sockets and anything past fd `65000` gets `Connection: close` so we don't blow past `LimitNOFILE=65535` with `EMFILE`.
- 0 failed requests across all 4.27m requests, and p95 stays at 10.63 ms at 128k vus.
